inline.s: The Symphony of the Universe
Recite and listen constantly, remember and practice constantly,
so that body and mind may gradually enter the Pure Land, and gradually arrive at utmost bliss.
Deepen faith and vows, and practice in accordance with the teaching.
Though for one lifetime you press forward with diligence and endure hardship, it is but a moment;
afterward you are born in the Land of Immeasurable Life, where bliss is without limit.

inline.s: [Deepening faith and vows, practicing as taught]
“Deepening faith and vows, practicing as taught”

is the very core of cultivation in the Pure Land school. If one truly achieves true faith and earnest vows, then one will certainly practice as taught, and this is the guarantee that ten thousand practitioners and ten thousand attain rebirth.
The essential purport of this sutra: arousing the bodhi mind and single-mindedly invoking the Buddha without interruption.

The Sutra of Immeasurable Life is the root scripture of the Pure Land school and the ultimate destination of the entire Tripiṭaka. It is truly the Tathāgata’s perfect teaching spoken from his own nature, the definitive teaching of the One Vehicle. It is the universal gate of all good, a symphony pervading the whole universe.

[One Vehicle] Also called the One Buddha Vehicle; the only teaching that can bring people to Buddhahood. “Vehicle” means a carriage, a metaphor for the Buddha’s teaching, which can carry people across to the far shore of nirvāṇa.
[Definitive teaching] Thorough and ultimate truth. [A symphony pervading the whole universe] The Buddha Speaks the Sutra of Immeasurable Life (Wei translation) says:
“Would you not hear the great sound of Immeasurable Life Buddha proclaimed throughout
(pervading all worlds)
the worlds, transforming
(teaching and converting)
sentient beings, or not
(an archaic way of writing “or not”)
? Ānanda replied: Indeed, I have heard it.”

Its Dharma-gate of “arousing the bodhi mind and single-mindedly invoking the Buddha without interruption” is perfect and direct, upāya in its ultimate sense, a single leap straight into the highest, most perfect and sudden teaching. It borrows Amitābha’s perfect fruition-enlightenment and makes it the causal mind of our own bodhi. Thought after thought one enters the Buddha’s fruition-enlightenment; mind after mind one abides in the Buddha’s right samādhi. Turning the back on dust and uniting with enlightenment, returning delusion to the real. The mind creates, the mind is — inconceivable.

[Arousing the bodhi mind] Giving rise to the great mind that “seeks the Buddha Way above (awakening, Buddhahood) and transforms sentient beings below.” [Single-mindedly invoking the Buddha without interruption]
invoking the Buddha unbrokenly and without any stray thoughts
(for details see
Single-Mindedly Invoking the Buddha Without Interruption
article)
Single-minded invocation without interruption is what
Master Shandao revealed: “Thought succeeds thought without interruption, to the end of this life.”
Master Shandao taught: “Where continuity holds, one is born
(when the end of life comes, one need only keep the thought of the Buddha continuous, unbroken by deluded thoughts, and one will attain rebirth in the Western Pure Land)
. If one can keep thought succeeding thought without interruption to the end of this life
(that is, one who practices this way for a whole lifetime —
that is, one who single-mindedly invokes the Buddha without interruption)
, then ten out of ten are born, a hundred out of a hundred are born.”
Here “continuity” means invoking the Buddha in every single thought without interruption.
Here “to the end of this life” means for one’s whole life.
For the detailed exposition of this teaching,
(for details see
Master Shandao’s Pure Land Teaching
) [The mind creates, the mind is] The Sutra of Contemplating the Buddha of Immeasurable Life says:
“This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha.”
[This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha] The Sutra of Contemplating the Buddha of Immeasurable Life says:

“All Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are the body of the Dharma-realm; they enter the thoughts of all sentient beings. Therefore, when you contemplate the Buddha, this mind is itself the thirty-two marks and eighty subsidiary marks.
This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha.
The Buddhas’ ocean of perfect and universal knowledge is born from the mind’s contemplation.”
(for annotated details see
Annotations on the Sutra of Contemplating the Buddha of Immeasurable Life
[Perfect and universal knowledge] One of the ten epithets of the Tathāgata.
The Sutra of Immeasurable Life has twelve translations in all, of which five survive:
1. The Sutra of Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment, translated under the Later Han by
Lokakṣema, abbreviated “the Han translation”;
2. The Sutra of Amitābha, the Tathāgata of Threefold Enlightenment, Sagely Honored One, Saving the Human Realm, translated by
Zhi Qian of Eastern Wu
, abbreviated “the Wu translation”;
[Amitābha]
Amita
, rendered in Chinese as “immeasurable.”

[Tathāgata of Threefold Enlightenment, Sagely Honored One] An honorific title of the Tathāgata. [Saving] To save and transform. [Human Realm] One of the six paths (heaven, human, asura, animal, hungry ghost, hell), that is, what is commonly called “the human world.” [The Sutra of Amitābha, the Tathāgata of Threefold Enlightenment, Sagely Honored One, Saving the Human Realm] means: the sutra of the Tathāgata Amitābha saving and transforming the human realm.
3. The Sutra of Immeasurable Life, translated under Cao Wei by
Saṅghavarman, abbreviated “the Wei translation”;
4. The Assembly of the Tathāgata of Immeasurable Life, translated under the Tang by
Bodhiruci, abbreviated “the Tang translation”;
5. The Buddha Speaks the Mahāyāna Sutra of Immeasurable Life’s Solemn Adornments, translated under the Song by
Dharmabhadra, abbreviated “the Song translation.”

The Sutra of Immeasurable Life is also the compendium of the many scriptures of the Pure Land school. It sets out in detail the causal ground and fruition of Amitābha Buddha’s attainment of Buddhahood, the direct retribution and adornments of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the faith, vows, practice, and realization of sentient beings who attain rebirth there, and the rejoicing in seeking and turning away from that the Pure Land practitioner undertakes. This is a scripture that those who invoke the Buddha must constantly recite, constantly hear, constantly remember, and constantly practice, so that body and mind may gradually enter the Pure Land and gradually arrive at utmost bliss.

Yet because this sutra has five translations whose contents are not entirely the same, it is hard for those who invoke the Buddha to study and cultivate them all regularly. Therefore, one after another, such great masters as Wang Longshu,
Peng Shaosheng
, Wei Moshen, and Xia Lianju brought forth the aspiration to gather them into a single volume, using refined and concise wording to
expound
and
promote
these five original translations, so as to aid daily
cultivation:
comprehending the sutra’s meaning
(the meaning of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life)
, deepening faith and vows, and practicing as taught.
These four collated editions are:
1. The Great Amitābha Sutra, collated under the Song by
Wang Rixiu (Wang Longshu), abbreviated “the Wang collated edition of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life”
2. The Sutra of Immeasurable Life (Peng Shaosheng’s Edited and Collated Edition), edited and collated in the early Qing by
Peng Shaosheng (Peng Jiqing, Peng Erlin) on the basis of the Wei translation, abbreviated “the Peng collated edition of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life”
3. The Mahā Amitābha Sutra, collated in the Xianfeng era of the Qing by
Wei Yuan (Wei Chengguan, Wei Moshen), abbreviated “the Wei collated edition of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life”
4. The Buddha Speaks the Mahāyāna Sutra of Immeasurable Life’s Solemn Adornments, Purity, and Equal Enlightenment, collated in the Republican era by
Xia Lianju, abbreviated “the Xia collated edition of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life”

Among these, The Buddha Speaks the Mahāyāna Sutra of Immeasurable Life’s Solemn Adornments, Purity, and Equal Enlightenment (the Xia collated edition of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life) was produced by Xia Lianju on the foundation of the previous three collated editions, strengthening what was strong and supplying what was lacking, so that the five original translations were most skillfully gathered into one, and divided into chapters. Its meaning is clear, its style graceful and fluent, easy to recite and easy to remember — especially suited to daily cultivation.
Yet because the Sutra of Immeasurable Life has five translations whose contents are not entirely the same, how to expound and promote these five translations became
an urgent problem to be solved in the study and practice of the Pure Land school.

As for the ways of expounding the five original translations, one may expound each in turn, or one may bring their contents together and expound them as a whole. In expounding them as a whole, one may unfold them at length; or one may expound them in refined and concise wording, explaining each passage through its vernacular rendering and annotations. The advantage of the latter is that it is easy to cultivate: on a first reading one may read everything closely, and afterward one need read only the classical text, consulting the vernacular renderings and annotations wherever something is unclear. Going further still, one may leave aside the vernacular renderings and annotations and read only the classical text, consulting the original translations as needed, or reading the original translations directly. — This is the method adopted by this book (the Collated Edition of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life).

This book aims to spread the Dharma and save sentient beings, and so takes expedient accommodation of the many as its principle: rather than starting a new stove of its own, it is based on the five original translations and consists of appropriate alterations made to the Xia collated edition of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life, which everyone already knows, and it is named the “Collated Edition” out of respect for the original work. For example, in the original book (the Xia collated edition), “The Sixth Chapter: Arousing the Great Vow” contains twenty-four vows that implicitly set out the forty-eight vows. The Collated Edition, drawing on the content of The Buddha Speaks the Sutra of Immeasurable Life (Wei translation) and The Buddha Speaks the Sutra of Amitābha, the Tathāgata of Threefold Enlightenment, Sagely Honored One, Saving the Human Realm (Wu translation), rewrites them as forty-eight vows, and changes the chapter title from
“The Sixth Chapter: Arousing the Great Vow” to “The Sixth Chapter: The Forty-Eight Vows.”

Again, for “The Seventeenth Chapter: The Merit of Springs and Pools,” the Collated Edition, drawing on The Buddha Speaks the Sutra of Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment (Han translation), The Buddha Speaks the Sutra of Amitābha, the Tathāgata of Threefold Enlightenment, Sagely Honored One, Saving the Human Realm (Wu translation), and The Assembly of the Tathāgata of Immeasurable Life (Tang translation), has made some additions and alterations to the original book.
[The Xia collated edition of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life] That is,
The Buddha Speaks the Mahāyāna Sutra of Immeasurable Life’s Solemn Adornments, Purity, and Equal Enlightenment, collated in the Republican era by
Xia Lianju, abbreviated “the Xia collated edition of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life”
Yet the Sutra of Immeasurable Life has five translations whose contents are not entirely the same. How, then, should these five translations be promoted and expounded?
There can be two ways of expounding them: first, expounding the five translations one by one; second, bringing the contents of the five translations together and expounding them as a whole.

In bringing the contents of the five translations together and expounding them as a whole, there can in turn be two methods: first, unfolding them at length; second, expounding them in refined classical wording, explaining each passage through its vernacular rendering and annotations.

The advantages of the latter method are that it is easy to recite, easy to remember, and convenient for cultivation. On a first reading one may read everything closely; afterward one need read only the classical text, consulting the vernacular renderings and annotations wherever something is unclear. Going further still, one may leave aside the vernacular renderings and annotations and read only the classical text, consulting the five translations (the scriptures) as needed, and then reading the five translations (the scriptures) directly.
Therefore this book adopts this latter method: expounding the sutra in refined classical wording, and explaining each passage through its vernacular rendering and annotations.

This book aims to spread the Dharma and save sentient beings, and so takes expedient accommodation of the many as its principle: rather than starting a new stove of its own, it is based on the five translations and consists of appropriate alterations made to the Xia collated edition of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life, which everyone already knows, and it is named the “Collated Edition” out of respect for the original work.

For example, in the original book (the Xia collated edition), “The Sixth Chapter: Arousing the Great Vow” contains twenty-four vows that implicitly set out the forty-eight vows. The Collated Edition, drawing on the content of The Buddha Speaks the Sutra of Immeasurable Life (Wei translation) and

The Buddha Speaks the Sutra of Amitābha, the Tathāgata of Threefold Enlightenment, Sagely Honored One, Saving the Human Realm (Wu translation), rewrites them as forty-eight vows, and changes the chapter title from
“The Sixth Chapter: Arousing the Great Vow” to “The Sixth Chapter: The Forty-Eight Vows.”

Again, for “The Seventeenth Chapter: The Merit of Springs and Pools,” the Collated Edition, drawing on The Buddha Speaks the Sutra of Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment (Han translation), The Buddha Speaks the Sutra of Amitābha, the Tathāgata of Threefold Enlightenment, Sagely Honored One, Saving the Human Realm (Wu translation), and The Assembly of the Tathāgata of Immeasurable Life (Tang translation), has made some additions and alterations to the original book.

The Collated Edition of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life, like all collated editions, is a comprehensive exposition and promotion of the five original translations in refined wording, and not a patchwork of texts. The Collated Edition, drawing on the content of The Buddha Speaks the Sutra of Immeasurable Life (Wei translation) and The Buddha Speaks the Sutra of Amitābha, the Tathāgata of Threefold Enlightenment, Sagely Honored One, Saving the Human Realm (Wu translation), rewrites them as forty-eight vows, and changes the chapter title from
“The Sixth Chapter: Arousing the Great Vow” to “The Sixth Chapter: The Forty-Eight Vows.”

Again, for “The Seventeenth Chapter: The Merit of Springs and Pools,” the Collated Edition, drawing on The Buddha Speaks the Sutra of Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment (Han translation), The Buddha Speaks the Sutra of Amitābha, the Tathāgata of Threefold Enlightenment, Sagely Honored One, Saving the Human Realm (Wu translation), and The Assembly of the Tathāgata of Immeasurable Life (Tang translation), has made some additions and alterations to the original book.

[A comprehensive exposition and promotion of the five original translations in refined wording] The exposition and promotion of the five original translations may proceed translation by translation, or may bring their contents together and expound them as a whole. In expounding them as a whole, one may unfold them at length; or one may expound them in refined wording, explaining each passage through its vernacular rendering and annotations (as the Collated Edition does). The advantage of the latter is that it is convenient for cultivation. On a first reading one may read everything closely; afterward one need read only the classical text, consulting the vernacular renderings and annotations wherever something is unclear. Going further still, one may leave aside the vernacular renderings and annotations and read only the classical text, consulting the original translations as needed, or reading the original translations directly.
The Three Character Classic begins by saying:
“Men at their birth are naturally good. Their natures are much the same; their habits become widely different.”

The meaning is that at the very beginning people are all good, and their natures are very much alike. But because of the differing environments in which each is steeped, their natures end up very far apart. Hence the story of Mencius’s mother moving house three times: by moving three times she chose a good environment in which to educate her child, and in the end brought forth a sage for his generation. From this we can see how immense the power of cultivation is:
near cinnabar one turns red, near ink one turns black
Ears steeped and eyes dyed, mind thinking and body acting — this is cultivation. Therefore one should “
recite and listen constantly, remember and practice constantly, so that body and mind may gradually enter the Pure Land and gradually arrive at utmost bliss
Constantly deepen faith and vows, and practice as taught
. Please remember firmly:
“Though for one lifetime you press forward with diligence and endure hardship, it is but a moment; afterward you are born in the Land of Immeasurable Life, where bliss is without limit.”
The Land of Ultimate Bliss is my home

. When reciting and listening, one should add visualization: the finer the visualization, the finer the perception; the truer the visualization, the truer the reality — until gradually one grasps the meaning and fathoms it in the heart. As the patriarchs said: a great tree that leans to the west must fall to the west; when the practitioner’s visualization is accomplished, at the end of life he is surely born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
In annotating sutras and treatises, the threefold division into the introduction, the main teaching, and the transmission serves as the rule:
1. The introduction sets out the reasons and conditions that gave rise to this sutra; this is the portion of the sutra’s origin.
2. The main teaching, spoken in response to those origins; this is the principal portion of the sutra.
3. The transmission entrusts the sutra for transmission, together with the benefits of transmitting and upholding it; this is the transmission portion of the sutra.
This piece is likewise divided into three great parts: the introduction, the main teaching, and the transmission:
I. Chapters one through three form the introduction.
II. Chapters four through forty-two form the main teaching.
III. Chapters forty-three through forty-eight form the transmission.
[Thus have I heard:]
This is what I (Ānanda) personally saw and heard:

[This is what I (Ānanda) personally saw and heard] Ānanda personally attended this assembly, and was moreover the one who requested it (the one who asked the Buddha to teach). [Ānanda] In full, Ānanda, one of the Buddha’s ten great disciples. He was the Buddha’s cousin, born on the night the Buddha attained enlightenment; later he left home to follow the Buddha, served him for twenty-five years, and was his attendant disciple. He was renowned as foremost in hearing much, and many scriptures were repeated by him at the compilations. [The ten great disciples] Śākyamuni Buddha’s ten great disciples, namely: Śāriputra, foremost in wisdom; Maudgalyāyana, foremost in spiritual powers; Subhūti, foremost in understanding emptiness; Ānanda, foremost in hearing much; Upāli, foremost in upholding the precepts; Aniruddha, foremost in the divine eye; Mahākāśyapa, foremost in ascetic practices; Pūrṇa, foremost in expounding the Dharma; Kātyāyana, foremost in discussion; Rāhula, foremost in secret practice. [Ascetic practices] A practitioner who abandons the three attachments to clothing, food, and dwelling. [The ascetic practices] The method of ascetic practice. In the daily life of one who cultivates the ascetic practices, twelve rules must be observed, called “the twelve ascetic practices.”
[At one time the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, in the Vulture Peak, together with a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus.]
At that time Śākyamuni Buddha was in the Vulture Peak in Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus.

[At one time] At that time. [Rājagṛha] The capital of Magadha in central India. [Vulture Peak] Also translated as Holy Vulture Mountain, or Spirit Mountain; it lies to the northeast of Rājagṛha and is a famous place where the Buddha often taught the Dharma. [Bhikṣu] A man who has left home and received full ordination. [Full ordination] Complete and perfect precepts: two hundred and fifty for bhikṣus and three hundred and forty-eight for bhikṣuṇīs. [Great bhikṣus] Describing these bhikṣus as all of high attainment. [Together] In one place.

[All these great sages had already reached the spiritual penetrations. Among them: the venerable Kauṇḍinya, the venerable Śāriputra, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the venerable Kāśyapa, the venerable Ānanda, and others, who were the foremost.]

All these great sages (the twelve thousand great bhikṣus in the assembly) had already attained the six penetrations (the divine eye, the divine ear, the knowledge of others’ minds, the knowledge of past lives, the power of unimpeded bodily travel, and the extinction of outflows). Among them the venerable Kauṇḍinya, the venerable Śāriputra, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the venerable Kāśyapa, the venerable Ānanda, and others were the foremost.

[All these great sages had already reached the spiritual penetrations] The Buddha Speaks the Sutra of Amitābha, the Tathāgata of Threefold Enlightenment, Sagely Honored One, Saving the Human Realm (Wu translation) says:
“The Buddha was in Rājagṛha, in the Vulture Peak, when there were twelve thousand great bhikṣus, all pure and of one kind, all arhats.”
Since arhats have cut off all afflictions and possess the six penetrations,

we know that “all these great sages had already reached the spiritual penetrations” refers to the twelve thousand great bhikṣus in the assembly, and not merely to the venerable Kauṇḍinya, the venerable Śāriputra, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the venerable Kāśyapa, the venerable Ānanda, and the others who were foremost.

[Had already reached the spiritual penetrations] Already possessed spiritual penetrations. [Spiritual penetration] Unfathomable transformation is called “spirit”; unimpeded thoroughness is called “penetration.” Here it refers to the six penetrations. [The six penetrations] The spiritual penetrations attained by the sages of the three vehicles (śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva), of six kinds: the divine eye, the divine ear, the knowledge of others’ minds, the knowledge of past lives, the power of unimpeded bodily travel, and the extinction of outflows. Specifically: first, the divine eye, which can see the sentient beings of the nine realms (hell, hungry ghost, animal, asura, human, heaven, śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva) and the marks of their suffering and bliss as they die here and are born there, and can see all the various forms and colors of every world without obstruction; second, the divine ear, which can hear the speech of suffering, bliss, sorrow, and joy of the sentient beings of the nine realms, and all the various sounds of the world; third, the knowledge of others’ minds, which can know what the sentient beings of the nine realms think in their minds; fourth, the knowledge of past lives, which can know one’s own past lives and deeds in one life, two lives, three lives, and on to a hundred thousand million lives, and can also know the past lives and deeds of every sentient being; fifth, the power of unimpeded bodily travel (the mastery of the body at will), by which the body can fly over mountains and seas without obstruction, vanishing from this realm and emerging in that, vanishing in that realm and emerging in this, making the great small and the small great, transforming at will; sixth, the extinction of outflows, which cuts off all afflictions (the delusions of view and thought); “outflow” means affliction. [The delusions of view and thought] Delusions of view and delusions of thought. Delusions of view are the errors of ordinary people in their views, such as the five wrong views of belief in a self, extreme views, wrong views, grasping at views as supreme, and grasping at precepts and practices as supreme; delusions of thought are the errors of ordinary people in their thinking, such as the afflictions of greed, anger, delusion, pride, and doubt. These two delusions are the root of sentient beings’ wandering through the three realms and suffering birth and death to no purpose; cutting them off, one can end birth and death and escape the three realms.

[The three realms] The realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm. The realm of desire is the world inhabited by sentient beings who have the two desires of sexual desire and the desire for food; it includes the six heavens of desire above, humans and animals in the middle, and hungry ghosts and hells below. The realm of form is the world inhabited by sentient beings who are free of the two desires of sexual desire and food but still have a body of form; it includes the eighteen heavens of the four dhyānas. The formless realm is the world inhabited by sentient beings who no longer have a body of form but abide with their consciousness in profound and wondrous samādhi; it includes the four formless heavens (the heaven of infinite space, the heaven of infinite consciousness, the heaven of nothingness, and the heaven of neither perception nor non-perception). These three realms are all the realm of ordinary people’s birth and death and rebirth, and so Buddhist practitioners first take escape from the three realms and the ending of birth and death as their aim. [The three vehicles] The śrāvaka vehicle, the pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the bodhisattva vehicle. The śrāvaka vehicle is also called the Small Vehicle; its practitioners, at the quickest in three lives and at the slowest in sixty kalpas, cultivate the Dharma of emptiness and in the end, hearing the Tathāgata’s spoken teaching, awaken to the truth of the Four Noble Truths, cut off the delusions of view and thought, and realize the fruit of arhatship. The pratyekabuddha vehicle is also called the Middle Vehicle; its practitioners, at the quickest in four lives and at the slowest in a hundred kalpas, break through ignorance and in the end awaken to the truth of the twelvefold dependent origination, realizing the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood. The bodhisattva vehicle is also called the Great Vehicle; its practitioners, over countless kalpas, cultivate the six pāramitās, and further, over a hundred kalpas, plant the causes of blessing for the thirty-two marks, realizing the supreme fruit of Buddhahood. [Foremost] Those who hold the highest place within the assembly.
Regarding the passage “all these great sages had already reached the spiritual penetrations,”
Master Huiyuan’s Profound Meaning of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life contains a question and answer that resolves students’ doubts:

“Question: ‘Ānanda, while the Buddha was in the world, dwelt on the ground of one still learning and had not attained the extinction of outflows; how can he be named among all these great sages who had already reached the spiritual penetrations?’ Explanation: ‘Ānanda, though he dwelt on the ground of one still learning, is not himself named a great sage who had reached the spiritual penetrations. It is in praise of the majority that the words are spoken: all these great sages had already reached the spiritual penetrations.’ Question: ‘Ānanda’s virtue was in truth not yet complete; why must he be listed among this assembly?’ Explanation: ‘Ānanda was the one who requested this assembly, and so must be distinctly listed. Moreover, Ānanda was of sharp faculties beyond the ordinary; though he dwelt on the ground of one still learning, he had accomplished immeasurable excellent and wondrous merit, and so is called a great sage. In the spiritual penetrations he had understood thoroughly and to the end, and so is also said to have already reached them.’”
Translation:
Question: “Ānanda, while the Buddha was in the world, dwelt on the ground of one still learning
(he had not attained the fruit of arhatship)

, and had not attained the penetration of the extinction of outflows. Why is the great assembly of bhikṣus, Ānanda included, described as ‘all these great sages who had already reached the spiritual penetrations’?” Explanation: “Though Ānanda dwelt on the ground of one still learning and cannot be called a great sage, nor said to have reached the spiritual penetrations, yet the others were all arhats; and so, following the vast majority, the praise is given, and therefore it is said, ‘all these great sages had already reached the spiritual penetrations.’”

Question: “Ānanda’s cultivated virtue was in fact not yet complete (he had not attained the fruit of arhatship); why then is he listed among these assembled sages?” Explanation: “Ānanda was the one who requested this assembly, and so he must be listed. Moreover, Ānanda was of sharp faculties beyond the ordinary: hearing one thing, he understood a thousand; once it passed his ear, he never forgot it. Though he dwelt on the ground of one still learning, he had already accomplished immeasurable excellent and wondrous merit, and so he is called a great sage. As for the spiritual penetrations, though Ānanda had not yet realized the penetration of the extinction of outflows, he had already understood them thoroughly, and so he too may be said to have reached them.”
Note: In the Lotus Sutra the Buddha tells the bodhisattvas:

“Ānanda and I, before the Buddha King of Space, alike aroused the mind of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi. Ānanda always delighted in hearing much; I always pressed forward with diligence. Therefore I have already attained anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi
(Buddhahood)
, while Ānanda protects my Dharma and also protects the Dharma-treasury of the future Buddhas, teaching and bringing the assembly of bodhisattvas to accomplishment.”
From this we know that Ānanda was no ordinary person.

[Dwelt on the ground of one still learning] It was only on the eve of the compilation of the scriptures that Ānanda attained arhatship and entered the ground of no more learning. So while the Buddha was in the world, Ānanda had not attained arhatship and dwelt on the ground of one still learning, and therefore had not attained the penetration of the extinction of outflows. [The ground of one still learning] The śrāvaka path has four fruits: stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship. The first three fruits are those of one still learning; the fourth fruit is that of no more learning. The stage of one still learning is the ground of learning. “Still learning” means one must go on advancing in study; “no more learning” means the way of study is complete and there is no further study to undertake.
[There were also the bodhisattvas Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, Maitreya, and all the bodhisattvas of the present auspicious kalpa, who all came to gather in the assembly.]
There were also the bodhisattvas Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, and Maitreya, and all the bodhisattvas of the present auspicious kalpa, who all came to take part in the assembly.

[Auspicious kalpa] The past great kalpa is called the Adornment kalpa, the future great kalpa is called the Star Constellation kalpa, and the auspicious kalpa is the present great kalpa. Because a thousand Buddhas appear in the world during this great kalpa, it is named the “auspicious kalpa.”

[Virtue in accord with Samantabhadra] All the great bodhisattvas who came to take part in the assembly were in accord with the virtue of Samantabhadra. [Samantabhadra’s virtue] The bodhisattva Samantabhadra’s practice and vows of compassion that universally saves and delivers all sentient beings.
Among the four great bodhisattvas (Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Guanyin, and Kṣitigarbha), Samantabhadra is renowned for “great practice.” The Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Vows says:

“At that time the bodhisattva mahāsattva Samantabhadra, having praised the Tathāgata’s supreme merit, addressed the bodhisattvas and Sudhana, saying: Good men, the Tathāgata’s merit — were all the Buddhas of the ten directions, through kalpas as numerous as the finest dust-motes of inexpressibly many Buddha-lands, to proclaim it in succession, it could never be exhausted. If you wish to accomplish this gate of merit, you should cultivate the ten vast practices and vows.”

[As numerous as the finest dust-motes of a Buddha-land] Grinding one Buddha-land into extremely fine dust-motes (the finest dust), the number of those dust-motes is called “as numerous as the finest dust-motes of a Buddha-land.” [The ten vast practices and vows] The ten kingly vows of Samantabhadra: 1. To pay homage and respect to all Buddhas; 2. To praise the Tathāgatas; 3. To make abundant offerings; 4. To repent of karmic obstacles; 5. To rejoice in others’ merit; 6. To request the turning of the Dharma-wheel; 7. To request the Buddhas to remain in the world; 8. To follow the Buddha in study always; 9. To accord with all sentient beings; 10. To universally transfer all merit.

[There were also sixteen eminent beings, namely: the bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, the bodhisattva Well-Considered, the bodhisattva Eloquent Wisdom, the bodhisattva Contemplating Non-Abiding, the bodhisattva Flower of Spiritual Penetration, the bodhisattva Light of Heroes, the bodhisattva Jewel Banner, the bodhisattva Supreme Wisdom, the bodhisattva Root of Stillness, the bodhisattva Wisdom of Faith, the bodhisattva Wisdom of Vows, the bodhisattva Fragrant Elephant, the bodhisattva Jewel of Heroes, the bodhisattva Abiding in the Middle, the bodhisattva Mastery of Practice, and the bodhisattva Liberation, who were the foremost.]

There were also sixteen great bodhisattvas (eminent beings), namely the bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, the bodhisattva Well-Considered, the bodhisattva Eloquent Wisdom, the bodhisattva Contemplating Non-Abiding, the bodhisattva Flower of Spiritual Penetration, the bodhisattva Light of Heroes, the bodhisattva Jewel Banner, the bodhisattva Supreme Wisdom, the bodhisattva Root of Stillness, the bodhisattva Wisdom of Faith, the bodhisattva Wisdom of Vows, the bodhisattva Fragrant Elephant, the bodhisattva Jewel of Heroes, the bodhisattva Abiding in the Middle, the bodhisattva Mastery of Practice, and the bodhisattva Liberation, who were the foremost.

[Eminent beings] Those who cultivate the right Dharma, that is, bodhisattvas. [The sixteen great bodhisattvas] As will be seen below, they are all bodhisattvas of the stage of equal enlightenment, second only to the Buddhas.

[All alike honored and cultivated the virtue of the great being Samantabhadra, were complete in immeasurable practices and vows, and abided peacefully in all Dharmas of merit. They roamed through the ten directions, practicing expedient means. They entered the Dharma-treasury and reached the ultimate shore.]

They all cultivated in accord with the virtue of the bodhisattva Samantabhadra (the ten kingly vows), were complete in immeasurable practices and vows, and abided peacefully in all practices and vows of merit. Going out to the worlds of the ten directions (roaming through the ten directions), they transformed sentient beings by expedient means suited to circumstances (practicing expedient means). They entered deeply into their own nature (entering the Dharma-treasury) and understood the way to Buddhahood (reaching the ultimate shore).

[Great being] A general designation for bodhisattva. [Practices and vows] Practice and vow. Practice and vow must accord: if there is only vow without practice, one can never reach the goal, never fulfill the vow. [The ten directions] East, south, west, north, southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, above, and below. [Expedient action] Acting according to circumstances, as expediency requires. [Expedient means] The devices, methods, or words adopted in order to guide and teach sentient beings. What is called “expedient means” is spoken in contrast to the real (the true mark of all dharmas). [The true mark of all dharmas] The actual condition of all dharmas (things and phenomena).
The actual condition of all dharmas is: ultimately empty, nothing whatsoever.
The Sutra of the Buddha-Treasury says:
“What is called the true mark of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, nothing whatsoever.”
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra says:
“All dharmas are like illusions; the Tathāgata, amid them, by the power of expedient means, is unstained by anything.”
The Lotus Sutra says:
“The bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates all dharmas as empty, as they truly are: not inverted, not moved, not retreating, not turning.”
(for details see
The True Mark of All Dharmas
) [Dharma-treasury] That is, the tathāgatagarbha (one’s own nature). [One’s own nature] The original state of the self-nature; also called the tathāgatagarbha (for details see
Mind, Self-Nature, Tathāgatagarbha

). [Equal and perfect enlightenment] Short for perfect and universal enlightenment, that is, the perfect realization of the Buddha-fruit. [Vowing to attain equal and perfect enlightenment in immeasurable worlds] It is said below:
(These sixteen great bodhisattvas)
all obtained the immeasurable merit and the sagely clarity of wisdom of the Buddhas.”

This shows that they, like the bodhisattvas Guanyin and Maitreya, are all bodhisattvas of the stage of equal enlightenment, whose next stage of practice is Buddhahood (the attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment); and so they vow to go to immeasurable worlds of the ten directions to attain Buddhahood.
Below is an account of how these sixteen great bodhisattvas will accomplish the Way through the eight marks of attainment (“vowing to attain equal and perfect enlightenment in immeasurable worlds”).

[The eight marks of attaining the Way] Manifesting eight marks to attain Buddhahood: descending from the Tuṣita heaven (coming down from the inner court of Tuṣita), entering the womb, being born, leaving home, subduing demons, attaining Buddhahood, turning the Dharma-wheel, and entering nirvāṇa (entering cessation, passing into extinction). [The Tuṣita heaven] The fourth of the six heavens of the realm of desire. [The inner court of Tuṣita] The inner court of the Tuṣita heaven, the dwelling place of a bodhisattva’s last body, from which he then descends to the human world and attains Buddhahood.

The following passage treats the first six of the eight marks: descending from Tuṣita (coming down from the palace of the Tuṣita heaven), entering the womb, being born, leaving home, subduing demons, and attaining Buddhahood.

[Vowing to attain equal and perfect enlightenment in immeasurable worlds: abandoning Tuṣita, descending into the royal palace, forsaking the throne to leave home, and practicing austerities in search of the Way. Making these manifestations in conformity with the world. By the power of concentration and wisdom, subduing the armies of Māra. Attaining the subtle and wondrous Dharma, achieving the supreme right enlightenment.]
They vow to attain Buddhahood in immeasurable worlds:

leaving the inner court of Tuṣita (descending from Tuṣita) and descending to be born in a royal palace in the human world (entering the womb, being born). Then forsaking the throne and leaving home (leaving home), practicing austerities in search of the Way. Making these manifestations is done in conformity with the world’s common views (because worldly people do not understand the true mark of all dharmas). By the power of concentration and wisdom they subdue the marauding armies of Māra (subduing demons). Attaining the profound and wondrous Dharma, they perfectly realize the Buddha-fruit (attaining Buddhahood).
The following four passages treat the seventh of the eight marks: turning the Dharma-wheel.

[Gods and humans take refuge and look up, requesting the turning of the Dharma-wheel. Always with the sound of Dharma, awakening the world; breaking the city of afflictions, destroying the moats of desire, washing away filth and defilement, making clear the pure white. Taming sentient beings, proclaiming the wondrous truth, storing up merit, revealing the field of blessing.]

After attaining Buddhahood, the sentient beings of heaven and the human world all took refuge in and relied upon him, requesting the Buddha to turn the great Dharma-wheel. Thereupon the Buddha always used the sound of Dharma to awaken the sentient beings of the world, teaching them to break down the city of afflictions, to destroy the desires that serve as the moat of that city of afflictions, to wash away the filth of deluded thoughts and attachment, and to make clear their own pure white nature. Taming sentient beings, proclaiming the wondrous truth, teaching them to accumulate merit, and showing them how to plant the field of blessing.

[Dharma-wheel] The Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma is like a great wheel that can crush all the afflictions of sentient beings. [Destroying the moats of desire] Destroying the desires that serve as the moat of the city of afflictions. Moat (
qiàn
) means a defensive trench around a city. [Making clear the pure white] Making clear the pure white nature.

[With the medicine of all dharmas, healing the three sufferings. Ascending the stage of consecration, receiving the bodhi prophecy. In order to teach bodhisattvas, acting as ācārya, always cultivating the corresponding immeasurable practices, maturing the bodhisattvas’ immeasurable roots of good, and all the immeasurable Buddhas together protecting and remembering them.]

With the various medicines of Dharma the Buddha healed sentient beings amid the three sufferings: those not yet saved he caused to be saved, and those already saved who had become bodhisattvas he consecrated with the ambrosial water of Dharma and gave them a prophecy: in what time, in what place, and as what Buddha they would attain Buddhahood. In order to teach these bodhisattvas he acted as their instructing master (ācārya), teaching them always to cultivate the corresponding immeasurable practices, maturing these bodhisattvas’ immeasurable roots of good; and the immeasurable Buddhas all protected and remembered them as well.

[Medicine of Dharma] The Buddhadharma is like medicine, able to cure the afflictions, suffering, and karmic obstacles of all sentient beings. [Healing the three sufferings] Healing the sentient beings amid the three sufferings:
“Sentient beings not yet saved, cause them to be saved; those already saved, cause them to attain Buddhahood.”

[Sentient being] Also called a living being, that is, every creature that has consciousness and feeling. [The three sufferings] First, the suffering of suffering, arising from such painful conditions as cold and heat, hunger and thirst. Second, the suffering of change, arising when a happy situation decays. Third, the suffering of formation, the suffering of all conditioned dharmas’ impermanence and shifting. [Ascending the stage of consecration, receiving the bodhi prophecy] This is
“those already saved, cause them to attain Buddhahood”

: the Buddha’s hand sprinkles their crowns and he gives them a prophecy: in what time, in what place, and as what Buddha they will attain Buddhahood. (Please note: in this passage the sixteen great bodhisattvas have already attained Buddhahood and are turning the Dharma-wheel, and so “ascending the stage of consecration, receiving the bodhi prophecy” is not consecration given to them, but what they do when transforming sentient beings.) [Ācārya] Also written ācārya, an instructing master.

[In all Buddha-lands they can manifest. Like a skilled illusionist who conjures many strange forms, yet within those forms there is in truth nothing to be obtained. These bodhisattvas are likewise so.]

These sixteen great bodhisattvas can manifest the eight marks of attaining the Way in all Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions. Like a skilled illusionist who conjures all manner of strange forms, yet within those forms there is in fact nothing at all (this is spoken with respect to the true mark of all dharmas).
[Buddha-land] A Buddha realm, a Buddha country. The land in which a Buddha dwells.

[Penetrating the nature of all dharmas, understanding the marks of sentient beings. Making offerings to all Buddhas, guiding the multitudes. Transforming and manifesting bodies like flashes of lightning, splitting the net of Māra’s views, untying all bonds. Causing them to rise far beyond the ground of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, entering the Dharma-gates of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Skillfully establishing expedient means, revealing the three vehicles.]

They (these sixteen Buddhas who accomplish the eight marks) penetrate the Dharma-nature, clearly awaken to the marks of sentient beings, and do not cling to the two extremes of existence and non-existence. They make offerings to all Buddhas and guide sentient beings. They (these sixteen Buddhas who accomplish the eight marks) transform and manifest bodies like lightning flashing on a pitch-black night to illumine the earth, tearing apart the net of Māra’s views and freeing sentient beings from the bonds of all deluded thoughts and afflictions. Teaching the One Vehicle Dharma, they cause them to rise far beyond the realms of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and to enter the three gates of liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. For those sentient beings who cannot yet accept the One Vehicle Dharma, they skillfully establish expedient means and reveal the three-vehicle teaching.
[Dharma-nature] The essential nature (substance) of all dharmas; another name for the true mark of all dharmas. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
“Sentient beings and lands share one Dharma-nature.”
The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom says:
“The Dharma-nature is, as said before, that each dharma is empty, and they are all one emptiness; this is the Dharma-nature.”

[The two extremes of existence and non-existence] Clinging to the extreme of existence and clinging to the extreme of non-existence are both wrong views. [The three gates of liberation] Three gates of wisdom entering the state of liberation: first, the gate of emptiness, comprehending that all dharmas are originally empty yet not clinging to emptiness; second, the gate of wishlessness, knowing that all dharmas are illusory existents and so making no wishes; third, the gate of signlessness, knowing that all dharmas are without marks and yet without non-marks, entering the middle way. [One Vehicle] Also called the One Buddha Vehicle; the only teaching that can bring people to Buddhahood. [The three vehicles] The śrāvaka vehicle, the pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the bodhisattva vehicle.
The following passage treats the last of the eight marks: entering nirvāṇa (entering cessation, passing into extinction).

[For those of middle and lesser capacity, manifesting extinction. Attaining the samādhis of no birth and no extinction, and attaining all the gates of dhāraṇī. At all times awakening into the Huayan samādhi, complete in the retention of a hundred thousand samādhis. Abiding in profound meditation, beholding all immeasurable Buddhas, and in the space of a single thought traveling through all Buddha-lands.]

They (these sixteen Buddhas who accomplish the eight marks), after turning the great Dharma-wheel, manifest the mark of entering cessation in order to benefit those of middle and lesser faculties. They realize the various samādhis of no birth and no extinction, and all the gates of total retention. At all times they awaken into the Huayan samādhi, complete in the retention of a hundred thousand samādhis. Abiding in profound meditation, they behold all immeasurable Buddhas and, in the space of a single thought, travel through all Buddha-lands.
[For those of middle and lesser capacity, manifesting extinction] Manifesting the mark of entering cessation in order to benefit those of middle and lesser faculties. The Lotus Sutra
Chapter on the Lifespan of the Tathāgata says:

“If the Buddha were to remain long in the world, people of scant virtue would not plant roots of good; poor and lowly, they would cling greedily to the five desires and enter the net of remembered imaginings and false views. If they saw the Tathāgata always present and not passing into extinction, they would give rise to arrogance and self-indulgence and harbor weariness and indolence, and could not give rise to the thought of how hard it is to meet a Buddha, nor to a mind of reverence.
Therefore the Tathāgata, though in truth he does not pass into extinction, manifests extinction.”

Not passing into extinction yet manifesting extinction, and so it is called a “manifestation.” He makes this manifestation for the sake of transforming those of middle and lesser faculties. As for those of superior faculties, who understand the true mark of all dharmas, they see that the Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere, is originally beyond birth and extinction — where is there any extinction? [Samādhi] Also written samādhi, that is, abiding the mind on a single object without distraction or torpor. [Attaining the samādhis of no birth and no extinction] Attaining the various samādhis of what is originally without birth or extinction (dharmas are originally unborn, and so also without extinction). Just above, immediately after “manifesting extinction,” it says “attaining the samādhis of no birth and no extinction,” showing that the Buddha’s entering extinction is a manifestation of impermanence for the sake of transforming those of middle and lesser faculties. Though he manifests the mark of extinction (nirvāṇa), in truth he is the unborn and undying, equal and ever-abiding suchness-dharmakāya.

[Dharmakāya] One of the three bodies. [The three bodies] The dharmakāya, the saṃbhogakāya, and the nirmāṇakāya. First, the dharmakāya, also called the body of self-nature, or the body of Dharma-nature: the unborn and undying true nature that everyone possesses inherently — only we sentient beings are deluded and do not reveal it, while the Buddha is awakened and has realized it. Second, the saṃbhogakāya, produced by the Buddha’s wisdom and merit, with a distinction between the body enjoyed by himself and the body enjoyed by others: the body enjoyed by himself is the body of inner realization and Dharma-bliss that the Buddha enjoys for himself, and the body enjoyed by others is the body manifested for the sake of teaching the bodhisattvas of the ten grounds. Third, the nirmāṇakāya, also called the body of response and transformation, or the body of transformation: the Buddha-body manifested in response to sentient beings’ capacities and conditions. [Dhāraṇī] Rendered in Chinese as “total retention,” that is, retaining all dharmas so that good dharmas are not lost and evil dharmas do not arise. [Huayan samādhi] Also called Huayan concentration. This samādhi is the great samādhi that encompasses the Dharma-realm and enters all Buddhadharmas.

The above has recounted how these sixteen great bodhisattvas will go to the worlds of the ten directions and accomplish the Way through the eight marks: descending from Tuṣita (coming down from the palace of the Tuṣita heaven), entering the womb, being born, leaving home, subduing demons, attaining Buddhahood, turning the Dharma-wheel, and entering nirvāṇa (entering cessation, passing into extinction).
The following two passages treat the present virtues of these sixteen great bodhisattvas.

[Attaining the Buddha’s eloquence, abiding in Samantabhadra’s practice. Skillfully discerning the languages of sentient beings, opening and revealing the ultimate reality, surpassing all dharmas of the world. The mind constantly and truly abides in the way of saving the world, and toward all things is freely at ease, becoming an uninvited friend to all kinds of beings. Receiving and upholding the Tathāgata’s profound Dharma-treasury, protecting the Buddha-seed nature so that it is never cut off.]

These sixteen great bodhisattvas attained the Buddha’s ability to expound the Dharma skillfully, and abide in the great practice of the bodhisattva Samantabhadra. They skillfully discern the languages of sentient beings and guide and teach the One Vehicle Dharma (opening and revealing the ultimate reality). They surpass all dharmas of the world, not grasping at marks, unmoved in suchness. Their minds constantly and truly abide in the way of transforming the world, and toward all things they are freely at ease (unfettered and unbound by any thing), becoming uninvited friends to all sentient beings. They protect and uphold the tathāgatagarbha, constantly causing the true nature to appear before them.

(Dwelling in Samantabhadra’s Practice) The passage above already said of these great beings that they “all alike cultivated the virtue of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra”; the present text says “dwelling in Samantabhadra’s practice,” showing that these great beings all abide in the great practice of Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
(Opening Up and Revealing the Real) To guide and teach the Dharma of ultimate truth, that is, the Dharma of the One Buddha Vehicle. The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Two,
“Skillful Means”: “The Tathāgatas appear in the world solely for the sake of the One Buddha Vehicle
(the Dharma of the One Vehicle)
, and for the sake of sentient beings they speak the Dharma; there is no other vehicle, neither a second nor a third.”

(The Multitude) All sentient beings. (A Friend Who Does Not Wait to Be Asked) A true friend does not wait to be invited, just as a loving mother instinctively cares for her infant. (To Receive and Uphold) To receive a teaching into one’s heart and practice it as taught. (The Tathāgata’s Profound Dharma-Store) The tathāgatagarbha. (The Buddha-Nature) One’s original nature.

Rousing great compassion, pitying sentient beings, proclaiming the Dharma with loving-kindness, granting the Dharma-eye; blocking the evil destinies, opening the gate of goodness. Toward every sentient being, looking upon them as oneself, rescuing and carrying them all across to the other shore. All alike attaining the Tathāgatas’ immeasurable merits and virtues, their wisdom and holy illumination beyond thought or speech.

They rouse the mind of great compassion, pity the sentient beings, lovingly proclaim the Dharma so that beings may gain right knowledge and right view (the Dharma-eye). They block the evil destinies and throw wide the gate of goodness. Looking upon all sentient beings as themselves, they rescue and carry them, delivering them to the other shore of nirvāṇa. All sixteen of these great bodhisattvas attain the Tathāgatas’ immeasurable merits and virtues, their wisdom and holy illumination beyond thought or speech.

Rousing great compassion, pitying sentient beings, proclaiming the Dharma with loving-kindness, granting the Dharma-eye; blocking the evil destinies, opening the gate of goodness. Toward every sentient being, looking upon them as oneself, rescuing and carrying them all across to the other shore” — this passage reveals the virtue of these sixteen great bodhisattvas, whose compassion is of one substance with all beings and whose loving-kindness has no conditions.

(Evil Destinies) Same in meaning as the evil paths. (Gate of Goodness) The gate by which one ends birth and death and realizes bodhi. (All alike attaining the Tathāgatas’ immeasurable merits and virtues, their wisdom and holy illumination) This shows that all sixteen of these great bodhisattvas are bodhisattvas of the stage of Equal Enlightenment, and that their merits and wisdom are therefore almost the equal of a Buddha’s. (Equal Enlightenment) In the fifty-two stages of the Mahāyāna, the fifty-first is named Equal Enlightenment: bodhisattvas who have perfected the ten grounds and are about to realize the fruit of Buddhahood, whose merits and wisdom are almost the equal of a Buddha’s, and who are therefore called “Equal Enlightenment.” They are also called “one life remaining,” because when this one life is exhausted (this one life of transformation birth-and-death) they will take the Buddha’s place.
Great bodhisattvas such as these, immeasurable and boundless, all assembled at one time.
Great bodhisattvas such as these, immeasurable and boundless, all came together to attend the Dharma assembly.

There were also five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, seven thousand pure-faith men, five hundred pure-faith women, and the gods and Brahma multitudes of the desire realm and the form realm, all gathered together in one great assembly.

There were also five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, seven thousand pure-faith men, five hundred pure-faith women, and the gods and Brahma multitudes of the desire realm and the form realm, who likewise came to attend the Dharma assembly.

(Bhikṣuṇī) A woman who has left home and received full ordination. (Pure-faith man) A man who has received the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts and possesses pure faith; in Sanskrit, an upāsaka. (Pure-faith woman) A woman who has received the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts and possesses pure faith; in Sanskrit, an upāsikā. (Brahma multitudes) The great assembly who cultivate the Brahma-life. (Brahma-life) Pure conduct, that is, the conduct of cutting off sexual desire.

blocks.text: 3. The Causal Ground of the Great Teaching

inline.s: At that time the World-Honored One, majestic in radiance, was like a mass of molten gold, and again like a bright mirror whose light and reflection flow through and through, within and without; he manifested a great radiance in many hundreds and thousands of transformations.

At this time the World-Honored One (Śākyamuni Buddha), majestic in the light of his virtue, blazed resplendent, like molten gold gathered into one mass, and again like a crystal-bright mirror whose light and reflection flow through and through, within and without, shining forth a great radiance, his forms and colors shifting and changing in many hundreds and thousands of ways.
(World-Honored One) An honorific title for the Buddha, because the Buddha is one honored by the whole world.

This was the World-Honored One, about to expound the supreme and subtle Pure Land Dharma-gate, manifesting auspicious signs and emitting light in a manner surpassing all others, in order to awaken Ānanda’s question and to cause those who heard to give rise to the thought of what is rare and hard to encounter, to practice as taught, and to seek rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

(Manifesting auspicious signs and emitting light in a manner surpassing all others) Before proclaiming the perfect and sudden sutras, the World-Honored One would always manifest auspicious signs and emit light. Yet the auspicious signs and light of this Dharma assembly were such as the Venerable Ānanda “from times past had never seen,” which shows that the Sutra of Immeasurable Life is an utterly perfect and sudden, incomparably supreme sutra, the rarest of all.

The Venerable Ānanda then thought to himself: today the World-Honored One’s physical body and sense faculties are joyful and pure, his countenance of light majestic, and the jeweled lands adorned within it — such a sight as he had never seen from times past. He rejoiced to behold it and gave rise to a heart of wonder.

The Venerable Ānanda then thought to himself: today the World-Honored One’s physical body and sense faculties are joyful and pure, his countenance of light majestic, and within the Buddha-light there appear the many jewel-adorned Buddha-lands — such a sight as he himself had never seen before. He rejoiced that he could behold it today and gave rise to a heart of rare and hard-won encounter.
(Sense faculties) The six faculties: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. (Joyful) Glad and happy.
(Majestic) Lofty, honored, and supreme.

Then rising from his seat, baring his right shoulder, kneeling long with palms joined, he addressed the Buddha: World-Honored One, today you have entered the great tranquil concentration, dwelling in the wondrous Dharma, dwelling in the conduct of the guide that all Buddhas dwell in, the supreme path. Past, future, and present — Buddha after Buddha is mindful of one another. Are you mindful of the Buddhas of past and future? Or are you mindful of the Buddhas of other directions in the present? Why is your majestic power so resplendent, your light and auspicious signs so wondrous and supreme? Pray reveal it to us.

Thereupon he rose at once from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt long with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha: World-Honored One, today you have entered the great tranquil concentration, dwelling in the wondrous Dharma, abiding in the conduct of the guide that all Buddhas dwell in, the supreme path. The Buddhas of past, future, and present — Buddha after Buddha is mindful of one another. Is the World-Honored One now mindful of the Buddhas of past and future? Or is he mindful of the Buddhas of other directions in the present? Why is his majestic power so resplendent, his light and auspicious signs so wondrous and supreme as this? Pray reveal it to the great assembly.
(To address) To speak respectfully to an elder or a superior. (Majestic power) Majestic virtue and spiritual power.

Thereupon the World-Honored One said to Ānanda: Well said! Well said! Because of pity and the wish to benefit and gladden sentient beings, you are able to ask about a meaning so subtle as this. This question of yours now surpasses by hundreds of thousands of times the merit of making offerings to the arhats and pratyekabuddhas of one world, and of giving gifts for many kalpas to the gods and humans and to the flying and crawling creatures. Why is that? Because the gods and humans and every living being of the future will, through your question, attain deliverance.

Thereupon the World-Honored One said to Ānanda: Well asked! Well asked! Out of pity and the wish to benefit and gladden sentient beings, you are able to ask about a meaning so subtle as this. This question of yours today surpasses by hundreds of thousands of times the merit of making offerings to the arhats and pratyekabuddhas of the whole world, and of giving gifts for many kalpas to the gods and humans and even to the flying and crawling creatures. Why? Because the gods and humans and all sentient beings of the future will, on account of this one question of yours, attain deliverance.

This question of yours now … the gods and humans and every living being of the future will all, through your question, attain deliverance” — this passage shows how magnificent the merit of Ānanda’s question is.
(Well said! Well said!) Well asked! Well asked! The World-Honored One was greatly delighted by Ānanda’s question and praised him highly.

(Pratyekabuddha) One who awakens by contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination and realizes the truth of emptiness. One who, in a Buddha’s lifetime, hears the Buddha teach the twelve links and awakens is called a “condition-enlightened one”; one who is born in an age without a Buddha and, contemplating the arising and ceasing of all dharmas, awakens by himself is called a “solitary-enlightened one.”
(The flying and crawling creatures:
xuān

) Flying or wriggling insects and the like. (Living being) A creature endowed with spirit. (Because all will, through your question, attain deliverance) Had Ānanda not asked, and the World-Honored One not revealed the Pure Land Dharma-gate, then sentient beings wishing to end birth and death and escape the round of rebirth would have to cut off every affliction (the delusions of view and thought); and in the age of the Final Dharma, scarcely one in a hundred million could succeed.
Yet in cultivating the Pure Land Dharma-gate, one need only have the right method and strive diligently — ten thousand cultivate and ten thousand go!
Ānanda, the Tathāgata, out of inexhaustible great compassion, pities
jīn

the three realms, and therefore appears in the world. He gloriously unfolds the teaching of the Way, wishing to rescue the multitude of beings and bestow upon them the benefit of truth. Hard to meet, hard to see, like the udumbara flower, rarely appearing. This question of yours now brings benefit to many.

Ānanda, the Tathāgata, out of inexhaustible great compassion, pities the sentient beings of the three realms, and therefore appears in the world. He gloriously unfolds the teaching of the great Way to rescue all the beings under heaven and bestow upon them the benefit of truth. The Tathāgata’s appearance in the world is hard to meet and hard to see, like the udumbara flower, rarely appearing. This question of yours today benefits sentient beings immensely.
(To pity: jīn) To have compassion for. (The multitude of beings:
méng

) The people, the populace. Méng is interchangeable with “máng.” Here “the multitude” means sentient beings. (Like the udumbara flower, rarely appearing) The Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra says:
“The udumbara flower: in our words, an auspicious sign; it appears once in three thousand years.”

(To benefit) To cause others to receive benefit. (This question of yours now brings benefit to many) Ānanda’s question today caused the Pure Land Dharma-gate to shine forth in the world, and for this we are endlessly grateful.

Ānanda, you should know that the Tathāgata, the Supremely Awakened One, has wisdom that is hard to measure and knows no obstruction. Within the space of a single thought he can dwell for immeasurable koṭis of kalpas, while his body and sense faculties neither increase nor decrease. Why is that? Because the Tathāgata’s concentration and wisdom are utterly unimpeded and without limit. He has attained the supreme mastery over all dharmas.

Ānanda, you should know that the Tathāgata, the Supremely Awakened One, has wisdom that is hard to measure and knows no obstruction whatsoever. He can, within a single thought, dwell for immeasurable koṭis of kalpas, while his eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind and all his faculties neither increase nor decrease in the least. Why? Because the Tathāgata’s concentration and wisdom are utterly unimpeded and inexhaustible, and because he has attained the supreme mastery over all dharmas.
(Supremely Awakened One) That is, the Supremely and Perfectly Awakened One, one of the Tathāgata’s ten honorific titles.
Ānanda, listen closely and ponder it well; I shall now explain it to you point by point.
Ānanda, you must listen attentively, receive it well and ponder it deeply; I shall now explain it to you point by point.

The Main Division is the principal part of this text, running from the fourth chapter through the forty-second. It is divided into four units: 1. Attaining Buddhahood and Establishing the Land; 2. The Dependent and the Direct Rewards of the Pure Land; 3. The Practice and Realization of Rebirth; 4. Yearning for the Pure Land and Turning from Saṃsāra.

blocks.text: 1. Attaining Buddhahood and Establishing the Land

inline.s: (Bhikṣu Dharmākara) Dharmākara is the name of Amitābha Buddha while in the causal ground.
(The Causal Ground) The whole stretch from the first arising of the bodhi-mind as an ordinary being studying the Buddha-Dharma until the perfection of Buddhahood is called the “causal ground.”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: In the past, immeasurable, inconceivable, incalculable kalpas ago, a Buddha appeared in the world named Lokeśvararāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Supremely and Perfectly Awakened One, Perfect in Wisdom and Conduct, Well-Gone One, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Beings, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One. He taught in the world for forty-two kalpas, and at that time he spoke the sutras and expounded the Way for the gods and the people of the world.

The Buddha said to Ānanda: In the past, immeasurable, inconceivable, incalculable kalpas ago, a Buddha appeared in the world named Lokeśvararāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Universally Knowing One (Supremely and Perfectly Awakened One), Perfect in Wisdom and Conduct, Well-Gone One, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Beings, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One. He taught and transformed sentient beings in the world for fully forty-two kalpas, constantly speaking the sutras and expounding the Way for the gods and the people of the world.

(Incalculable) Without end or limit; describing an exceedingly long span. (Supremely and Perfectly Awakened One) Also translated “Universally Knowing One”; in Sanskrit, samyak-saṃbuddha. One of the Tathāgata’s ten titles. (The Tathāgata’s ten titles) The Buddha has ten honorific titles: 1. Tathāgata, one who comes by the way of Suchness to accomplish perfect awakening; 2. Arhat, worthy of the offerings of gods and humans; 3. Universally Knowing One, truly and universally knowing all dharmas; 4. Perfect in Wisdom and Conduct, fully endowed with the three insights — the insight of past lives, the divine eye, and the extinction of outflows — and with the five practices of the noble, the Brahma-life, the divine, the infant, and the sick; 5. Well-Gone One, freely and well departed, entered into nirvāṇa; 6. Knower of the World, able to understand the principle and the facts of all worlds; 7. Unsurpassed One, the one who is supreme; 8. Tamer of Beings, able to tame and guide great beings who cultivate the right path; 9. Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha being the guide of all gods and humans; 10. Buddha, World-Honored One, the Buddha being the one honored in common by the whole world.

There was a great king of a country named Ratnavatī, who, hearing the Buddha teach the Dharma, rejoiced and understood, and forthwith brought forth the mind of the unsurpassed true Way. He abandoned his country and gave up his throne, went forth as a śramaṇa, and was named Dharmākara, cultivating the bodhisattva path.

At that time there was a king of a great country named Ratnavatī, who, hearing the Buddha teach the Dharma, gave rise to great joy, suddenly awakened, and forthwith brought forth the mind of the unsurpassed true Way. Thereupon he abandoned the throne, shaved his head and left home, and was named Dharmākara, cultivating the bodhisattva path.
(King Ratnavatī) The Sutra of Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment Spoken by the Buddha (the Han translation) says:

“The Buddha taught the sutras and expounded the Way for the gods and the people of the world, and none could surpass him. When King Ratnavatī heard the sutras and the Way, he rejoiced and understood, and thereupon abandoned his royal throne and went forth as a bhikṣu.”

(Forthwith) In a moment. (Śramaṇa) A general term for one who leaves home to cultivate the Way. (The bodhisattva path) That is, the six pāramitās; this is the path that perfects benefit for oneself and others and accomplishes the fruit of Buddhahood. (The six pāramitās) The six dharmas by which one may cross from this shore of the afflictions of birth and death to the other shore of the peace of nirvāṇa: giving, precepts, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and prajñā. Giving overcomes stinginess and greed; precepts overcome transgression; patience overcomes anger; diligence overcomes indolence; meditative concentration overcomes distraction; prajñā overcomes delusion. The details are as in the table below:

He was supremely talented, courageous, and wise, surpassing all the world; in faith, understanding, and clear memory he was foremost in all things. He also had supreme conduct and vows, and the powers of mindfulness and wisdom, which strengthened his mind so that it was firm and unmoved. In his cultivation he was so diligent that none could surpass him.

Bhikṣu Dharmākara’s talent was extraordinary, his courage and diligence unmatched, his mind clear and his wisdom bright, far surpassing all people in the world. His acceptance in faith and understanding, his grasp of principle and power of memory, were likewise foremost in all things. He also had supreme conduct and vows, together with the five powers — faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom — which strengthened his mind so that before hardship, peril, threats, and enticement he remained firm and unmoved. In his cultivation he was so diligent that no one could surpass him.

(The powers of mindfulness and wisdom) Here the power of mindfulness and the power of wisdom stand for the five powers. (The five powers) The powers of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. The power of faith is the growth of the root of faith, able to destroy all wrong beliefs; the power of diligence is the growth of the root of diligence, able to destroy the body’s indolence; the power of mindfulness is the growth of the root of mindfulness, able to destroy all wrong thoughts; the power of concentration is the growth of the root of concentration, able to destroy all scattered thinking; the power of wisdom is the growth of the root of wisdom, able to destroy all the delusions of the three realms (the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm).
He went to where the Buddha was, bowed his head to the ground, knelt long, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and with gāthās praised the Buddha and brought forth his vast vows.

He came to the dwelling place of Lokeśvararāja Tathāgata, bowed his head to the ground and knelt long, joined his palms toward the Buddha, praised the Buddha in verse, and brought forth his vast vows.
(Gāthā) In Chinese, “verse.”
The verses say:
The Tathāgata’s subtle form is peerless in beauty,
His boundless light illumines the ten directions,
yào
(Sun, moon, fire, and jewels all hide their radiance) The light of the sun, the moon, fire, and precious jewels is altogether hidden and no longer seen.
The World-Honored One can utter a single sound,
And can manifest a single wondrous form,

The World-Honored One can expound with a single sound, and each kind of sentient being hears it in its own language, and all are able to understand the principle he speaks. He can also manifest a single subtle form, so that each kind of sentient being sees the very form of its own kind that it delights in most.
I vow to attain the Buddha’s pure voice,
Proclaiming the gate of precepts, concentration, and wisdom.

(Precepts and concentration) Here a short form of “precepts, concentration, and wisdom.” (Precepts, concentration, and wisdom) Also called the three trainings, or the three outflow-free trainings. Precepts means to stop evil conduct; concentration means to settle the mind on one point; wisdom means to destroy delusion and realize truth. Precepts can subdue the mind of greed; concentration can subdue the mind of anger; wisdom can subdue the mind of deluded folly. Holding these three dharmas of precepts, concentration, and wisdom can counteract the three poisons and accomplish the fruit of Buddhahood; hence they are called the “three outflow-free trainings.”
Wisdom vast and deep as the sea,
Surpassing the boundless gates of evil destinies, swiftly reaching the ultimate shore of bodhi.
(Free of dust and toil) Without affliction. “Dust and toil” is another name for affliction. (The ultimate shore of bodhi) The perfection of Buddhahood.
Ignorance, greed, and anger forever gone;
And like the Buddhas of boundless ages past,

(Ignorance, greed, and anger forever gone; delusion exhausted and faults gone, by the power of samādhi) By the power of samādhi, cutting off utterly the greed, anger, and delusion of ignorance, together with the delusions of view and thought and every fault.
Able to save every world,
Always practicing giving, precepts, and patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom — the six pāramitās.
(The six pāramitās) That is, the six pāramitās, also called the six perfections.
Beings not yet delivered, may they be delivered;
Though one made offerings to holy ones as many as the sands of the Ganges, it would not equal firm and valiant seeking of true awakening.

(Beings not yet delivered, may they be delivered; those already delivered, may they attain Buddhahood) Sentient beings who have not yet ended fragmentary birth-and-death are caused to end fragmentary birth-and-death; sentient beings who have already ended fragmentary birth-and-death are caused to end transformation birth-and-death and attain Buddhahood. (Fragmentary birth-and-death) Sentient beings in the three realms and six paths, whose lifespans are all limited and whose bodies are all distinct, as brought about by good and evil karma; hence their birth and death is called “fragmentary birth-and-death.” One who ends fragmentary birth-and-death escapes the round of rebirth and leaves the three realms. Cutting off utterly the delusions of view and thought is to end fragmentary birth-and-death, as with the arhats. (Transformation birth-and-death) The sages of the three vehicles have already cut off the delusions of view and thought and have ended fragmentary birth-and-death. In the course of cultivating the Way, deluded thoughts gradually cease and realization gradually increases; each period of this shift from delusion to realization differs from the last. The passage from the earlier period into the later is exactly like one birth and death, and is therefore called “transformation birth-and-death.” One who ends transformation birth-and-death perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood. (Though one made offerings to holy ones as many as the sands of the Ganges, it would not equal firm and valiant seeking of true awakening) Though one made offerings to Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it would still not equal one’s own resolute and valiant seeking of the path to Buddhahood, because this can deliver sentient beings all the more widely. (The sands of the Ganges) The Ganges is a great river of India, and its waters hold much fine sand; when the Buddha spoke the Dharma he would often use the number of the fine sands of the Ganges to describe an extremely large number.
I vow to abide in samādhi,
Attaining a vast and pure dwelling,

(A vast and pure dwelling) The pure Buddha-land that Bhikṣu Dharmākara brought about upon becoming a Buddha — the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. (Attaining a vast and pure dwelling) The Buddha-land is brought about by the Buddha’s perfect merit, virtue, blessing, and wisdom. (Without equal) Having nothing that can be compared with it.
Beings of every kind revolving in the paths of rebirth,
Ever bearing a loving heart to rescue sentient beings,
(To rescue sentient beings) To uproot the suffering of sentient beings.
My resolve is firm and powerful;
Though this body should remain amid every suffering, such a vow and mind will never retreat.
(Gathering in the Buddha-lands) To design the Buddha-land.

When Bhikṣu Dharmākara had spoken these verses, he addressed the Buddha: I am now cultivating the bodhisattva path and have already brought forth the mind of unsurpassed perfect awakening; I vow to become a Buddha, and to make all things as they are in a Buddha.
