I pray that the Buddha will broadly proclaim the sutras and the Dharma for me; I shall receive and uphold them, cultivate as taught, uproot the root of birth and death with all its toil and suffering, and swiftly accomplish unsurpassed, perfect, and universal awakening.

When Bhikṣu Dharmākara had spoken these verses, he addressed the Buddha: I now cultivate the bodhisattva path and have already brought forth the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and universal awakening; I vow to become a Buddha, in all things as the Buddha is. I pray that the Buddha will broadly proclaim the sutras and the Dharma for me; I shall receive and uphold them, cultivate as taught, uproot the root of birth and death with all its toil and suffering, and swiftly realize the fruit of Buddhahood (swiftly accomplish unsurpassed, perfect, and universal awakening).

(Unsurpassed Awakening) A short form of unsurpassed, perfect, and universal awakening. (Unsurpassed, perfect, and universal awakening) The Chinese translation of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi: the highest, truest, most equal, and most universal awakening, that is, the utterly perfect fruit of Buddhahood.

When I become a Buddha, may my wisdom and radiance, the land I dwell in, and the name of its teacher all be heard throughout the ten directions. May gods and humans and the flying and crawling creatures who come to be born in my land all become bodhisattvas. If I establish this vow and it surpasses the lands of countless Buddhas, may I then attain it?

When I become a Buddha, may my wisdom and radiance, the Buddha-land I establish, and the name of its teacher (Amitābha Buddha) all be heard throughout the ten directions. May gods and humans and even the flying and crawling creatures who come to be born in my land all become bodhisattvas. If I establish this vow and it is to surpass the lands of countless Buddhas, can it be attained?

(The name of the teacher) The name of the teacher, that is, the name of Bhikṣu Dharmākara after he becomes a Buddha (Amitābha Buddha). The Sutra of the Buddha’s Explanation of the Passing of Humanity as Told in the Sutra of Amitāyus, the Buddha of the Threefold Buddha-Land (the Wu translation) says:
“When I later become a Buddha, may the name of the teacher be heard in all the eight directions, above and below, throughout countless Buddha-lands, and may none fail to hear and know my name.”

Buddha Lokeśvararāja then spoke the Dharma to Dharmākara: Suppose the great ocean were measured out by one man with a peck-measure; though kalpas passed, he could still reach the bottom. If a person seeks the Way with utmost sincerity and does not cease his diligence, he will surely accomplish the fruit — what vow could he fail to attain?

Buddha Lokeśvararāja then spoke the Dharma to Dharmākara: Suppose the great ocean were measured out by one man with a peck-measure; though many kalpas passed, he could still reach the bottom of the sea. If a person seeks the Way with utmost sincerity and does not cease his diligence, he will surely succeed — what vow could he fail to accomplish?

(Utmost sincerity) A heart perfectly sincere and perfectly firm. When utmost sincerity is brought forth, the sagely fruit is certain to be contained in it, for the cause penetrates the sea of the fruit, and flower and fruit are simultaneous; one need only be diligent — what vow could fail to be attained?
(To accomplish the fruit)
To succeed.

Reflect for yourself: by cultivating what means can you accomplish the adornment of a Buddha-land? As to how you should cultivate, you yourself should know. A pure Buddha-land you must gather in for yourself.

Reflect for yourself: by cultivating what can you accomplish such an adorned Buddha-land? As to how you should cultivate, you yourself should know. A pure Buddha-land you must gather in (design) for yourself.
(By cultivating what means) Here “skillful means” refers to the method of cultivation. (Can you accomplish the adornment of a Buddha-land) Can you accomplish the adornment of your Buddha-land.

(You must gather in for yourself) You must gather in (design) it for yourself. The Buddha-land is brought about by the Buddha’s perfect merit, virtue, blessing, and wisdom. Chapter Four, “The Causal Ground of Dharmākara,” says:
“Attaining a vast and pure dwelling, supremely adorned beyond all comparison.”

And first of all one must make a concrete design for this vast and pure dwelling, supremely adorned beyond all comparison, and draw up a detailed “blueprint.” For this Bhikṣu Dharmākara spent fully five kalpas.

Dharmākara said: This meaning is vast and profound, beyond my reach. I only pray that the Tathāgata, the Arhat and Universally Knowing One, will broadly set forth the immeasurable wondrous lands of all Buddhas. If I may hear such dharmas and ponder and cultivate them, I vow to fulfill what I have wished.

Dharmākara said: This meaning is too profound, beyond my reach. I only pray that the Tathāgata will broadly set forth the immeasurable wondrous lands of all Buddhas. If I may hear such dharmas and ponder and cultivate them, I vow to fulfill what I have wished.

(The Tathāgata, the Arhat and Universally Knowing One) That is, Tathāgata, Arhat, and Universally Knowing One; among these, Arhat and Universally Knowing One are the second and third of the Tathāgata’s ten titles.

Buddha Lokeśvararāja, knowing his loftiness of mind and the depth and breadth of his vows, thereupon proclaimed for him the two hundred and ten koṭis of Buddha-lands, with their merit, adornment, purity, vastness, and perfection. In accordance with his wish, he manifested them all to him. When he spoke this Dharma, a thousand koṭis of years passed.

Buddha Lokeśvararāja, knowing that Dharmākara’s wisdom was lofty and bright and his vows deep and vast, proclaimed for him the merit, adornment, purity, vastness, and perfection of the two hundred and ten koṭis of most exemplary Buddha-lands. And in accordance with his wish, he displayed them to him one by one. When he spoke this Dharma, a thousand koṭis of years passed.
(Thereupon proclaimed for him the two hundred and ten koṭis of Buddha-lands)
The Sutra of Immeasurable Life Spoken by the Buddha (the Wei translation) says:

“Thereupon Buddha Lokeśvararāja broadly proclaimed for him the two hundred and ten koṭis of Buddha-lands, the good and evil of their gods and humans, and the coarse and wondrous quality of their lands, and in accordance with his wish displayed them all to him.”

At that time, when Dharmākara heard what the Buddha said and beheld it all, he brought forth the unsurpassed and supreme vow. Upon the good and evil of those gods and humans and the coarse and wondrous quality of those lands, he pondered to the very end. Then, with mind made one, he chose what he desired and formed his great vows.

At that time Dharmākara heard Buddha Lokeśvararāja set forth each one, and saw each manifested Buddha-land, and thereupon brought forth the unsurpassed and supreme vow to establish his own Buddha-land. Upon the good and evil of the gods and humans of those two hundred and ten koṭis of Buddha-lands, the coarse and wondrous quality of their lands, and all the rest, he pondered and investigated thoroughly. With mind made one, he chose what he himself desired and thereby formed the guiding outline for the establishment of his Buddha-land (he formed his great vows).

He sought diligently and earnestly, reverently and carefully maintained it, cultivated merit and virtue, and fulfilled five kalpas. Upon the merit and adornment of those two hundred and ten koṭis of Buddha-lands he was clear and thoroughly comprehending, as though they were a single Buddha-land. The Buddha-land he gathered in surpassed them all.

Then, valiant and diligent, he sought earnestly and tirelessly cultivated merit and virtue for fully five kalpas, completing the blueprint of the Buddha-land he was to establish (given form in the forty-eight vows). Upon the merit and adornment of those two hundred and ten koṭis of Buddha-lands he was clear and thoroughly comprehending, as though they were a single Buddha-land. And the Buddha-land he was to establish surpassed them all.
(The blueprint of the Buddha-land he established) The Commentary on the Sutra of Immeasurable Life says:
“Now when a bodhisattva establishes a pure land, it is like a master craftsman building a great city: he first thinks it over and draws it out.
(a particle introducing the sentence)
When a bodhisattva establishes a pure land, it is like a master craftsman building a great city: he first thinks it over and draws it out.
Five kalpas of contemplation: thus he draws it.”
(Translation: When a bodhisattva establishes the Buddha-land of his own Buddhahood, it is like a master architect building a great city: he first, in deep thought, draws up the blueprint.
Bhikṣu Dharmākara, through five kalpas of seeking and cultivating virtue, drew up the blueprint of his own Buddha-land.)

When he had gathered it in, he again went to where Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja was. He bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, circled the Buddha three times, stood with palms joined, and said to the World-Honored One: I have accomplished the pure conduct of the adorned Buddha-land.

When Bhikṣu Dharmākara had completed the blueprint of the Buddha-land he was to establish, he came once more to the dwelling place of Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja. He bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, circled the Buddha three times, stood with palms joined, and said to the Buddha: I have accomplished the pure conduct of the blueprint of the Buddha-land.

(I have accomplished the pure conduct of the adorned Buddha-land) After Buddha Lokeśvararāja had proclaimed and displayed for Bhikṣu Dharmākara the merit, adornment, purity, vastness, and perfection of the two hundred and ten koṭis of Buddha-lands, he spent five kalpas drawing up the blueprint of his own Buddha-land (given form in the forty-eight vows). After he made the blueprint public (set forth the forty-eight great vows), he accumulated merit and virtue and passed through immeasurable, inconceivable, incalculable kalpas, and so perfectly accomplished the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
(He accumulated merit and virtue and passed through immeasurable, inconceivable, incalculable kalpas, and so perfectly accomplished the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss) Earlier the text said:
“Immeasurable, inconceivable, incalculable kalpas ago, a Buddha appeared in the world named Lokeśvararāja Tathāgata”
“when he spoke this Dharma, a thousand koṭis of years passed”
(Bhikṣu Dharmākara)
cultivated merit and virtue and fulfilled five kalpas”
, and later the text says:
“Dharmākara became a Buddha, named Amitābha. Since his Buddhahood, ten kalpas have passed”

. Therefore the time from Bhikṣu Dharmākara’s accumulation of merit and virtue to his perfect accomplishment is: immeasurable, inconceivable, incalculable kalpas, minus a thousand koṭis of years, five kalpas, and ten kalpas — which, from the standpoint of modern mathematics, is still immeasurable, inconceivable, incalculable kalpas. Ordinarily the time for a bodhisattva to cultivate the Way to Buddhahood is three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas, yet the time for Bhikṣu Dharmākara to cultivate the Way to Buddhahood was immeasurable, inconceivable, incalculable kalpas — how many, many, many times more than three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas this is! This shows how great the difficulty of establishing the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss was, truly beyond thought,
and therefore especially supreme
. Therefore Amitābha Buddha is
“the most honored among lights, the king of Buddhas”
, and the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss
“surpasses the lands of countless Buddhas”

. Where the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss established by Amitābha Buddha is most supreme is this: other Dharma-gates require one to cut off every affliction (the delusions of view and thought) before one can end birth and death and escape the round of rebirth; the Pure Land Dharma-gate, however, requires only that at the end of life one recite the name of Amitābha Buddha ten times in unbroken succession, and one can thereby feel Amitābha Buddha appear before one and guide one to rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and so end birth and death and escape the round of rebirth (see in full
“The Conditions for Rebirth”
). Comparing the difficulty of the two is like the distance between heaven and an abyss! Hence it is said:
“In the Final Dharma, of a hundred million times a hundred million people who cultivate, hardly one attains the Way; only by relying on reciting the Buddha’s name can one cross birth and death.”
Moreover, once reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss one attains the stage of non-retrogression, straight through to Buddhahood. Therefore the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:

“This question of yours now surpasses by hundreds of thousands of times the merit of making offerings to the arhats and pratyekabuddhas of one world, and of giving gifts for many kalpas to the gods and humans and to the flying and crawling creatures. Why is that? Because the gods and humans and every living being of the future will, through your question, attain deliverance.”

(Three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas) The time for a bodhisattva to attain Buddhahood. Kalpas are of three sizes, great, medium, and small; the kalpa spoken of here is the great kalpa, hence “three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas.” As for the number of years in one asaṃkhyeya kalpa, if one reckons ten thousand times ten thousand as one yi and ten thousand yi as one zhao, then one asaṃkhyeya kalpa equals ten million times ten thousand times ten thousand times ten thousand times ten thousand times ten thousand times ten thousand zhao of great kalpas.

The Buddha said: Excellent! Now is precisely the time. You should set it forth in full, so that the assembly may rejoice. And may the great assembly, having heard this Dharma, gain great benefit. May they be able to cultivate and gather in Buddha-lands, fulfilling their boundless great vows.

Buddha Lokeśvararāja said: Excellent! Now is precisely the time. You should set it forth in concrete detail, so that the assembly may rejoice. And may the great assembly, having heard this Dharma, gain great benefit, and be able to cultivate and gather in Buddha-lands of their own, so as to fulfill their boundless great vows of attaining Buddhahood and establishing lands.
Dharmākara said: I only pray that the World-Honored One will hear and consider with great compassion.
Dharmākara respectfully said to the Buddha: I only pray that the World-Honored One will hear and consider with great compassion.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be hells, hungry ghosts, or animals in my land, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(01. Vow that the Land Have No Evil Destinies)
If I become a Buddha
, and there should be hells, hungry ghosts, or animals in my land, may I not attain Buddhahood.
(May I not attain perfect enlightenment) Then may I not become a Buddha.
“If, when I attain Buddhahood, the humans and gods of my land should, after the end of their lives, fall again into the three evil destinies, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(02. Vow that They Not Fall Again into Evil Destinies)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the devas and humans in my land, after the end of their lives, were again to fall into the three evil destinies, then may I not become a Buddha.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not all possess bodies of true golden hue, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 03: Bodies of True Golden Color)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the devas and humans in my land did not all possess bodies of true golden hue, then may I not become a Buddha.
[All]
entirely.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should differ in form and color and have the fair and the ugly, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 04: Neither Fair nor Ugly)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the devas and humans in my land differed in form and color and had the fair and the ugly, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Fair and ugly] Good and not good. Here “ugly” means that a thing is not good, as in “ugly field.” [Have the fair and the ugly] Having distinctions of good and not good.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not obtain the power of knowing past lives, down to knowing the affairs of a hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of kalpas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 05: The Power of Knowing Past Lives)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the devas and humans in my land did not obtain the power of knowing past lives, down to knowing the affairs of a hundred thousand kotis of kotis of kalpas, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Nayuta] The name of a number, equal to what is now called a koti.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not obtain the divine eye, down to seeing a hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 06: The Power of the Divine Eye)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the devas and humans in my land did not obtain the divine eye, down to seeing a hundred thousand kotis of kotis of Buddha-lands, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not obtain the divine ear, down to hearing all that a hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of Buddhas have spoken and receiving and upholding it all, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 07: The Power of the Divine Ear)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the devas and humans in my land did not obtain the divine ear, down to hearing all that a hundred thousand kotis of kotis of Buddhas have spoken and receiving and upholding it all, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not obtain the knowledge of others’ minds, down to knowing the thoughts of the beings in a hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 08: The Power of Knowing Others’ Minds)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the devas and humans in my land did not obtain the knowledge of others’ minds, down to knowing the thoughts of the beings in a hundred thousand kotis of kotis of Buddha-lands, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not obtain the power of unimpeded travel, so that in the space of a single thought they cannot go beyond a hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 09: The Unobstructed Power of Travel)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the devas and humans in my land did not obtain the power of unimpeded travel, so that in the space of a single thought they cannot go beyond a hundred thousand kotis of kotis of Buddha-lands, then may I not become a Buddha.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should give rise to thoughts and be covetous of and calculating about their bodies, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 10: No Coveting or Calculating about the Body)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the devas and humans in my land gave rise to thoughts and were covetous of and calculating about their bodies, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Covetous of and calculating about the body] Falsely clinging to a self and a body (falling into the view of a body) and, with greed, calculating and measuring love and hate, compliance and opposition, and the like. Ordinary people in cultivation mostly fall into the view of a body, and the view of a body stands first among the delusions of view; if the delusions of view are not cut off, one cannot enter the stream of the sages. [Delusions of view] The delusions of view are the errors of ordinary people in their views, such as the five wrong views: the view of a body, extreme views, evil views, the view of grasping at views, and the view of grasping at precepts and observances.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not abide in the certain state and must reach extinction, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 11: Abiding in the Right and Certain State)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the devas and humans in my land did not abide in the right and certain state and must reach nirvāṇa, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Certain state] An abbreviation of “the right and certain state.” [The three groups] The three groups are three classes of beings: the right and certain group (abbreviated as the certain group), the wrong and certain group, and the uncertain group. The right and certain group refers to the class of beings who will certainly realize enlightenment; the wrong and certain group refers to the class of beings who in the end cannot realize enlightenment; the uncertain group refers to the class of beings between right and wrong, who may or may not realize enlightenment.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, my light should be measurable, down to not shining upon a hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 12: Immeasurable Light)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and my light were limited, down to not shining upon a hundred thousand kotis of kotis of Buddha-lands, then may I not become a Buddha.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, my lifespan should be measurable, down to a hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of kalpas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 13: The Buddha’s Immeasurable Life)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and my lifespan were limited, down to a hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of kalpas, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the sravakas in my land should be countless, so that even if the beings of a trichiliocosm all became pratyekabuddhas and together calculated for a hundred thousand kalpas, they could know their number, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 14: Countless Sravakas)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the sravakas in my land were countless, so that even if the beings of a trichiliocosm all became pratyekabuddhas and together calculated for a hundred thousand kalpas, they could know their number, then may I not become a Buddha.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the lifespan of the devas and humans in my land should be beyond measure. Except that, by their original vows, they may make it long or short
as they wish. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 15: The Measureless Lifespans of the Beings)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the lifespan of the devas and humans in my land were without limit, except that, by their original vows, they may make it long or short as they wish; if it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.
[If it were not so] If it were not thus.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should so much as hear of any evil name, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 16: Hearing No Evil Name)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the devas and humans in my land so much as heard of any evil name, then may I not become a Buddha.
so much as hear of any evil name
] In the Land of Ultimate Bliss not even the name of evil exists, so how could there be evil deeds? To such a degree does the surpassing excellence of the Land of Ultimate Bliss reach!
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the countless Buddhas of the worlds of the ten directions should not all praise and proclaim my name, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 17: Praise by All the Buddhas)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the countless Buddhas of the worlds of the ten directions did not all praise and proclaim my name, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the beings of the ten directions, with utmost sincerity and joyful faith, desire to be born in my land, and even for ten thoughts, should not be born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. Only those who have committed the five rebellious acts and slandered the right Dharma are excepted.
(Vow 18: Certain Rebirth through Ten Thoughts)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the beings of the ten directions, with utmost sincerity and joyful faith, desire to be born in my land, and even for ten thoughts, should not be born there, then may I not become a Buddha. Only those who have committed the five rebellious acts and slandered the right Dharma are excepted.

[Utmost sincerity] A heart utterly sincere and utterly firm. [Even for ten thoughts] This is an abbreviated way of saying “even at the point of death, with ten thoughts in unbroken succession, invoking my name.” As to the precise meaning of “even for ten thoughts” in the eighteenth vow, Master Daochuo teaches in the Collection of the Land of Peace:
“If there are beings who, though they have done evil all their lives,
at the time of death, with ten thoughts in unbroken succession, invoke my name
, and should they not be born, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”
(For details, see
“Even for Ten Thoughts”
“The Eighteenth Vow”
) [Ten thoughts in unbroken succession] Without admixture of false thoughts, invoking the name of Amitābha ten times with mind succeeding mind. Master Tanluan teaches:
“With no other mind intermingled
(without admixture of false thoughts)
, mind succeeding mind
(mind following upon mind
, even for ten thoughts, this is called ten thoughts in unbroken succession.”
He also says:
“Ten thoughts in unbroken succession at the point of death, and one attains rebirth.”
(For details, see
“Master Tanluan’s Pure Land Teaching”

) [The five rebellious acts] Five kinds of offenses that run utterly counter to principle: killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, killing an arhat, shedding the Buddha’s blood, and causing division in the Sangha. Because these five are acts of extreme evil, and because committing any one of them brings a fall into the Avici Hell, they are also called “uninterrupted karma.”

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the beings of the ten directions who have aroused the bodhi mind and cultivated all merits, and who with utmost sincerity make vows and desire to be born in my land, should at the end of their lives not be met and surrounded by a great assembly appearing before them, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 19: Rebirth through Utmost Sincerity)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the beings of the ten directions who have aroused the bodhi mind and cultivated all merits, and who with utmost sincerity make vows and desire to be born in my land, should at the end of their lives not be met and surrounded by a great assembly appearing before them, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the beings of the ten directions who hear my name, are mindful of my land, plant the roots of all virtues, and with utmost sincerity dedicate them, desiring to be born in my land, should not have their wish fulfilled, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 20: Certain Rebirth through Mindfulness)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the beings of the ten directions who hear my name, are mindful of my land, plant the roots of all virtues, and with utmost sincerity dedicate them, desiring to be born in my land,
should not have their wish fulfilled
, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Roots of virtue] That is to say, roots of goodness. Virtue means goodness; root means foundation. The merit of all good practices is the foundation of the fruition of Buddhahood. The Lotus Sutra says:
“Before all the Buddhas, they planted the roots of all virtues.”
The Sutra of Immeasurable Life says:
“They extinguished all outflows and planted the roots of all virtues.”

[Dedication] “Turning one’s own roots of virtue toward a certain goal”: concentrating and directing the roots of virtue one has created toward some purpose, so that it may be quickly accomplished. For example, one dedicates all the good one has cultivated through the three karmas (bodily, verbal, and mental), and even such merits as repentance and entreaty, to all beings of the Dharma realm, that they may together be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. The Commentary on the Treatise on Rebirth says:
“Dedication means turning one’s own merit and giving it universally to beings, that together they may see the Tathagata Amitābha and be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss
(the Land of Ultimate Bliss)
Master Shandao’s Verses on Arousing the Vow and Taking Refuge in the Three Treasures say:
“May this merit of mine be given equally to all, that together we may arouse the bodhi mind and be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss.”
(The Liturgy of the Four-Part Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra)
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not all possess the thirty-two marks of a great man, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 21: The Thirty-Two Marks)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the devas and humans in my land did not all possess the thirty-two marks of a great man, then may I not become a Buddha.

[The thirty-two marks of a great man] Also called the thirty-two marks of a great man: 1. level soles; 2. wheels with a thousand spokes on the soles; 3. long, slender fingers; 4. soft hands and feet; 5. webbed hands and feet; 6. full and rounded heels; 7. high and well-formed insteps; 8. calves (
shuàn

) like those of a royal deer; 9. hands reaching past the knees; 10. the pudendum concealed like that of a horse; 11. breadth and length of body; 12. blue-black hair pores; 13. body hair curling upward; 14. a golden body; 15. a constant light of ten feet; 16. fine, smooth skin; 17. the seven places full and rounded; 18. full armpits; 19. a body like a lion; 20. an upright body; 21. full and rounded shoulders; 22. forty teeth in the mouth; 23. teeth white, even, and close-set;

24. four teeth pure white; 25. jawbones (the palate bones that hold the teeth) like those of a lion; 26. the fluids of the throat attaining the finest flavor; 27. a broad, long tongue; 28. a pure, far-reaching Brahma voice; 29. dark blue eyes; 30. eyelashes like those of a royal bull; 31. a white tuft between the eyebrows; 32. a fleshy mound on the crown of the head. [Dark blue (
gàn
)] A color black with red showing through.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas of other Buddha-lands who come to be born in my land should not ultimately reach the stage of one life to Buddhahood; except that, by their original vows, for the sake of beings they don the armor of their vast vows and go to other worlds, freely delivering all. Roaming through all Buddha-lands, cultivating the bodhisattva path, accumulating the roots of virtue, and making offerings to the Tathagatas of the ten directions. Teaching and transforming beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
causing them to stand in the unsurpassed, right, and true way,
transcending the practices of the ordinary stages
and manifesting the cultivation of the virtue of Samantabhadra. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 22: One Life to Buddhahood)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the bodhisattvas of other Buddha-lands who come to be born in my land should not ultimately reach the stage of one life to Buddhahood; except that, by their original vows, for the sake of beings they don the armor of their vast vows and go to other worlds, freely delivering all beings. Roaming through all Buddha-lands, cultivating the bodhisattva path, accumulating the roots of virtue, and making offerings to the Tathagatas of the ten directions. And they teach and transform beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, causing them to stand in the unsurpassed, right, and true way, transcending the practices of the ordinary stages and manifesting the cultivation of the virtue of Samantabhadra. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.

[One life to Buddhahood] Filling the Buddha’s place when this one life ends: this is another name for the bodhisattva of the last body (the bodhisattva of equal enlightenment). For example, Maitreya Bodhisattva, who now dwells in the inner court of the Tusita Heaven, is a bodhisattva of one life to Buddhahood. All the beings who attain rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss have immeasurable lifespans and attain Buddhahood in this one life; the “one life” spoken of refers to one life of segmentary birth-and-death. But the “one life” in “filling the Buddha’s place when this one life ends” refers to one life of transformation birth-and-death. [Donning the armor of their vast vows] They don the great armor adorned by the merit of their vast vows. [Causing them to stand in the unsurpassed, right, and true way] Teaching and transforming them to cultivate the Pure Land Dharma-gate. “The unsurpassed, right, and true way”

refers to the Pure Land Dharma-gate. Because the Pure Land Dharma-gate is perfect and direct, expedient and ultimate, a single leap that goes straight in, the most perfect and sudden of all, it is called the unsurpassed, right, and true way. Master Hanshan teaches:

“The one gate of the Pure Land embraces all three capacities alike, and the sudden and the gradual enter together; there is no capacity it does not gather in. This is what is meant by transcending the three realms sideways,
and it is the most supreme Dharma-gate
He also teaches:
“The Buddha spoke of many expedient gates for cultivating the way out of birth and death, but only reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land
is the most swift and essential
(Dream-Play Collection
Preface to Pointing the Way Home to the Pure Land)

[Transcending the practices of the ordinary stages] Surpassing the cultivation of the common path, in which one advances stage by stage in fixed order. In cultivation on the common path, a bodhisattva must pass through fifty-two stages from ordinary being to Buddhahood, namely: the ten stages of faith, the ten stages of abiding, the ten stages of practice, the ten stages of dedication, the ten stages of ground, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment. But one who cultivates the Pure Land Dharma-gate and is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss sees the Buddha when the flower opens, awakens to the non-arising, and obtains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas, ascending to the eighth ground. [The eighth ground] The eighth of the bodhisattva’s ten grounds, called the Ground of Immovability. On this ground the bodhisattva abides in the patience of the non-arising of dharmas, cuts off all exertion, and puts body and mind to rest, like empty space; he accomplishes the perfection of vow and, with a mind of nirvāṇa, is still and unmoving, and so it is called the “Ground of Immovability.” [The ten grounds] The Ground of Joy, the Ground of Freedom from Defilement, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Supreme Difficulties, the Ground of Manifestation, the Ground of Far-Reaching, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Good Wisdom, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud. These are the fifth of the ten sets in the bodhisattva’s fifty-two stages of cultivation. On these ten grounds one gradually opens the realm of Buddhahood and accomplishes the wisdom of all modes; they already belong to the stage of the sages, and so they are also called the “ten sages.” [The three wisdoms] The wisdom of all, the wisdom of the paths, and the wisdom of all modes. The wisdom of all is the wisdom by which sravakas and pratyekabuddhas understand the general characteristic of all dharmas, the general characteristic being the true nature of all dharmas; the wisdom of the paths is the wisdom by which bodhisattvas understand the various gates of practice; the wisdom of all modes is the wisdom by which the Buddha comprehends both the general and the particular characteristics of all dharmas and, teaching and cutting off delusion, transforms beings.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, should make offerings to all Buddhas and, in the space of a single meal, be unable to reach a hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 23: Making Offerings to All Buddhas)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the bodhisattvas in my land, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, made offerings to all Buddhas and, in the space of a single meal, were unable to reach a hundred thousand kotis of kotis of Buddha-lands, then may I not become a Buddha.
[The space of a single meal] The time of one meal. The Perfection of Wisdom Sutra
Fascicle 347

Chapter of Entrustment arranges lengths of time in order: one day and night, one day, half a day, one hour (equal to two hours today), the space of a meal, a moment, an instant, the space of a breath.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land, presenting the roots of virtue before all Buddhas, should not obtain the offerings they require as they wish, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 24: Offerings as They Wish)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the bodhisattvas in my land, presenting the roots of virtue (roots of goodness) before all Buddhas, should not obtain the offerings they require as they wish, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Offerings] Also called offerings. Things such as incense, flowers, food and drink, banners, and canopies offered to Buddhas and bodhisattvas. The Ratnakuta Sutra says:
“Bearing
(jī, to carry)
wondrous offerings, they present them to the Tathagata and the great assembly.”
The Lotus Sutra says:
“In ages to come, with all manner of offerings, they will make offerings and serve.”
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land should be unable to expound the wisdom of all, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 25: Expounding the Wondrous Wisdom)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the bodhisattvas in my land were unable to expound the wisdom of all, then may I not become a Buddha.
[The wisdom of all] The wisdom that understands the general characteristic of all dharmas, the general characteristic being the true nature of all dharmas.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land should not obtain bodies of vajra Narayana, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 26: The Body of Narayana)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the bodhisattvas in my land did not obtain bodies of vajra Narayana, then may I not become a Buddha.
[The body of vajra Narayana] A body as solid as vajra and with strength as measureless as that of the god Narayana; hence it is called the body of vajra Narayana.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, all the myriad things of the devas and humans in my land should not be adorned, pure, luminous, and beautiful, with forms and colors most extraordinary, reaching the subtle and the ultimate, beyond all reckoning; and if any being there, even one who has attained the divine eye, should be able to discern and distinguish their names and numbers, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 27: All Adorned and Pure)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and all the myriad things of the devas and humans in my land were not adorned, pure, luminous, and beautiful, with forms and colors most extraordinary, reaching the subtle and the ultimate, beyond all reckoning; and if any being in my land, even one who has attained the divine eye, should be able to discern and distinguish their names and numbers, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Names and numbers]
The number of the items.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land, even those of scant merit, should be unable to know and see the bodhi tree of that land, with its immeasurable light and color and its height of four million li, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 28: Knowing and Seeing the Bodhi Tree)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the bodhisattvas in my land, even those of scant merit, were unable to know and see the bodhi tree of that land, with its immeasurable light and color and its height of four million li, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land who receive, read, recite, uphold, and expound the sutras and Dharma should not obtain eloquence and wisdom, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 29: Wisdom through Reciting the Sutras)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the bodhisattvas in my land who receive, read, recite, uphold, and expound the sutras and Dharma did not obtain eloquence and wisdom, then may I not become a Buddha.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the wisdom and eloquence of the bodhisattvas in my land should be measurable, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 30: Unmeasurable Wisdom and Eloquence)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the wisdom and eloquence of the bodhisattvas in my land were measurable, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the land should not be pure and should not reflect and reveal all the measureless, countless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions as a bright mirror reveals the face. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 31: Revealing the Ten Directions)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the land were not pure and did not reflect and reveal all the measureless, countless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions as one sees one’s face in a bright mirror. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, from the ground upward and up to the sky, the palaces, towers, terraces, pools, streams, flowers, and trees, all the myriad things in my land, should not be formed in common from measureless jewels and fragrances. Adorned and wondrous, surpassing all devas and humans. Their fragrance pervades the worlds of the ten directions. Bodhisattvas who smell it all cultivate the practices of the Buddha. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 32: The Wondrous Adornment of Jewel Fragrance)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and from the ground upward and up to the sky, the palaces, towers, terraces, pools, streams, flowers, and trees, all the myriad things in my land, were not formed in common from measureless jewels and fragrances. Adorned and wondrous, surpassing all devas and humans. Their fragrance pervades the worlds of the ten directions. Bodhisattvas who smell it all cultivate the practices of the Buddha. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the beings of the measureless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions whose bodies are touched by my light should not be supple in body and mind, surpassing devas and humans, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 33: Supple Bodies upon Touching the Light)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the beings of the measureless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions whose bodies are touched by my light were not supple in body and mind, surpassing devas and humans. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the beings of the measureless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who hear my name should not obtain the bodhisattva’s patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas and the profound dharani, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 34: Attaining Patience upon Hearing the Name)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the beings of the measureless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who hear my name did not obtain the bodhisattva’s patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas and the profound dharani, then may I not become a Buddha.

[The patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas] Abbreviated as the patience of non-arising: penetrating the truth that all dharmas are originally unborn, that sentient and insentient alike arise from conditions and have no nature of their own, and are empty just as they are; and therefore abiding in the non-arising without the mind stirring. [No nature of their own] Nature means substance; all dharmas have no substantial reality (and so are illusory), and this is called having no nature of their own. The Lotus Sutra says:
“One knows that all dharmas are always without a nature of their own.”
The Surangama Sutra says:
“All illusions are accomplished as without a nature of their own.”
[Dharani]
Holding all dharmas, so that good dharmas are not lost and evil dharmas do not arise.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, I cause there to be no women in my land. If women wish to come and be born in my land, they immediately become men. The countless devas and humans, and even flying and crawling creatures, who come to be born in my land, are all born by transformation in lotuses in seven-jeweled pools, and when grown are all bodhisattvas and arhats. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 35: No Women, Born in Lotuses)
“If I were to become a Buddha

I would cause there to be no women in my land. If women wish to come and be born in my land, they immediately become men. The countless devas and humans, and even flying and crawling creatures, who come to be born in my land, are all born by transformation in lotuses in seven-jeweled pools, and when grown are all bodhisattvas and arhats. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.
[I cause there to be no women in my land]
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on Amitābha, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and the Deliverance of Human Beings (the Wu Translation) says:

“The second vow: when I attain Buddhahood, may there be no women in my land. If women wish to come and be born in my land, they immediately become men. The countless devas and humans, and flying and crawling creatures, who come to be born in my land, are all born by transformation in lotuses in seven-jeweled pools of water. When grown they are all bodhisattvas and arhats, countless in number. If I obtain this vow, then I shall attain Buddhahood; if I do not obtain this vow, I shall never attain Buddhahood.”
[Countless] Without end.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the hosts of bodhisattvas in the measureless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, having heard my name, should after the end of their lives always cultivate the pure conduct until they attain the way of Buddhahood. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 36: Always Cultivating Pure Conduct)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the hosts of bodhisattvas in the measureless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, having heard my name, should after the end of their lives always cultivate the pure conduct until they attain the way of Buddhahood. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Pure conduct]
Pure and clean action.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans of the measureless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, having heard my name, should bow with all five limbs to the ground, pay homage with head bowed, rejoice, have faith, and delight in cultivating the bodhisattva path, so that devas and humans of the world all pay them reverence. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 37: Homage by Devas and Humans)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the devas and humans of the measureless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, having heard my name, should bow with all five limbs to the ground, pay homage with head bowed, rejoice, have faith, and delight in cultivating the bodhisattva path, so that devas and humans of the world all pay them reverence. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land, wishing to obtain clothing, should have it arrive as soon as they think of it. Wondrous robes praised by the Buddha and in accord with the Dharma should naturally be on their bodies. If there were any cutting, sewing, dyeing, or washing, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 38: Wondrous Robes upon Thought)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the devas and humans in my land, wishing to obtain clothing, had it arrive as soon as they thought of it, with wondrous robes praised by the Buddha and in accord with the Dharma naturally on their bodies. If there were any cutting, sewing, dyeing, or washing, then may I not become a Buddha.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not enjoy bliss equal to that of a bhiksu who has exhausted the outflows, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 39: Bliss Like the Exhaustion of Outflows)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the devas and humans in my land did not enjoy bliss equal to that of a bhiksu who has exhausted the outflows, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Exhaustion of outflows] The complete cutting off of all afflictions (the delusions of view and of thought). Outflow is another name for affliction. [The delusions of view and of thought] The delusions of view and the delusions of thought. The delusions of view are the errors of ordinary people in their views, such as the five wrong views: the view of a body, extreme views, evil views, the view of grasping at views, and the view of grasping at precepts and observances; the delusions of thought are the errors of ordinary people in their thinking, such as the afflictions of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt. These two delusions are the root of the beings’ revolving in birth and death; cut them off, and one can end birth and death and escape the round.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land who wish, as they please, to see the measureless, adorned, and pure Buddha-lands of the ten directions, should have their wish fulfilled at once and see them all reflected in the jeweled trees, as one sees one’s face in a bright mirror. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 40: Revealing the Lands in the Trees)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the bodhisattvas in my land who wish, as they please, to see the measureless, adorned, and pure Buddha-lands of the ten directions, had their wish fulfilled at once and saw them all reflected in the jeweled trees, as one sees one’s face in a bright mirror. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, should until they attain Buddhahood have deficient or imperfect faculties, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 41: Faculties Without Deficiency)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, should until they attain Buddhahood have deficient or imperfect faculties, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, should all obtain the samādhi of purity and liberation. Abiding in this samādhi, in the space of a single thought of intent, they make offerings to measureless, inconceivable World-Honored Buddhas without losing their concentration. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 42: Abiding in Samādhi and Making Offerings)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, all obtained the samādhi of purity and liberation. Abiding in this samādhi, in the space of a single thought of intent, they make offerings to measureless, inconceivable World-Honored Buddhas without losing their concentration. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, should after the end of their lives be born into honored and noble families. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 43: Merit upon Hearing the Name)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, should after the end of their lives be born into honored and noble families. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, should rejoice and leap for joy, cultivate the bodhisattva path, and be complete in the roots of virtue. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 44: Complete in the Roots of Virtue)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, rejoiced and leaped for joy, cultivated the bodhisattva path, and were complete in the roots of virtue (roots of goodness). If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, should all obtain the universal and equal samādhi. Abiding in this samādhi, until they attain Buddhahood they always see all the measureless, inconceivable Buddhas. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 45: The Universal and Equal Samādhi)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, all obtained the universal and equal samādhi. Abiding in this samādhi, until they attain Buddhahood they always see all the measureless, inconceivable Buddhas. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.
[The universal and equal samādhi] One who cultivates this meditative concentration can see all Buddhas within the concentration.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land, according to their vows and aspirations, should not naturally hear the Dharma they wish to hear. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 46: Hearing the Dharma as Vowed)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the bodhisattvas in my land, according to their vows and aspirations, did not naturally hear the Dharma they wish to hear. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, should not immediately attain non-retrogression, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 47: Non-Retrogression upon Hearing the Name)
“If I were to become a Buddha
and the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, did not immediately attain the stage of non-retrogression, then may I not become a Buddha.
[The stage of non-retrogression] Also written Avaivartika, or A-pi (
pí

) pa-chih. This is the name of a stage of the bodhisattva, which a bodhisattva can reach only after cultivating for one great asamkhyeya kalpa. From that point on there is only advance step by step until Buddhahood, with no retrogression in between. The Amitābha Sutra Spoken by the Buddha says:
“In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, all beings who are born there are Avaivartika.”

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, should not immediately attain the first, second, and third patient acceptances, and in the Buddha-Dharma should be unable immediately to attain non-retrogression, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 48: Attaining the Three Patient Acceptances)
“If I were to become a Buddha

and the hosts of bodhisattvas of other lands, having heard my name, did not immediately attain the first, second, and third patient acceptances, and in the Buddha-Dharma were unable immediately to attain non-retrogression, then may I not become a Buddha.

[The first, second, and third patient acceptances] Namely the patience of sound, the patience of compliance, and the patience of the non-arising of dharmas. For the explanations of these three kinds of patience, see in detail “Fifteen, The Place of Enlightenment.”
“The Buddha said to Ānanda: At that time, when Dharmakara Bhiksu had spoken these vows, he spoke in verse:
I founded a resolve surpassing the world, and I shall surely reach the unsurpassed Way
(I shall certainly realize the fruit of Buddhahood)
, and if these vows are not fulfilled
(if these forty-eight vows are not fulfilled)
, I vow not to attain equal enlightenment
(I vow not to become a Buddha)
“Vow of Transcending the World” refers to the vow spoken earlier: “It shall surpass and excel the lands of countless Buddhas.”
Again, as a great giver I appear, to succor all the poor and distressed; I shall grant every being relief, and give them long nights free from sorrow and care.
I shall bring forth every root of goodness, and accomplish the fruit of bodhi; when I attain perfect enlightenment, my name shall be Immeasurable Life.
“Immeasurable Life” is the Buddha’s name; its transliteration is Amitābha.
When beings hear this name
(when beings hear this name),
all shall come to my land; like the Buddha’s golden body, their wondrous marks shall be complete.
Likewise with a heart of great compassion, benefiting every kind of being,
them
free from desire and deep in right mindfulness, with pure wisdom cultivating the pure life.
“Every kind of being” means sentient beings.
May my light of wisdom shine universally over lands in the ten directions, dispel the gloom of the three defilements, and with clarity rescue all from hardship and adversity.

“Three defilements” is another name for the three poisons, namely greed, anger, and delusion. “The gloom of the three defilements” is the darkness of the three poisons. “With clarity rescue all from hardship and adversity” means using the light of wisdom to rescue beings from all their hardships and adversities.
All shall cast off the suffering of the three paths, and extinguish the darkness of all afflictions; I shall open for them the eye of wisdom, and they shall attain a body of light.

“Three paths” are the path of blood, the path of knives, and the path of fire. The path of blood is the animal realm, because animals constantly dwell where they are killed or devour one another; the path of knives is the realm of hungry ghosts, because hungry ghosts constantly dwell where hunger, or swords, whips, and staves oppress them; the path of fire is the hell realm, because hells constantly dwell in freezing ice or where fierce flames scorch and sear. These three paths are another name for the three evil paths.
Shut
(shut)
all evil paths, and open
(throw open)
the gate of good destinies; for all beings I open the Dharma-store, and broadly bestow the treasure of merit.

“Evil paths”: for ordinary people in the world, the evil paths mean the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals. Here the evil paths are the five evil paths spoken of in the Sutra of Immeasurable Life (Wei translation) — hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and gods. “Block all evil paths” means cutting off the road of birth-and-death and transmigration. The Sutra of Immeasurable Life (Wei translation) says:

“Each should strive with diligence, and seek deliverance with his own effort. You shall surely transcend and pass beyond, and be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss. Cutting across the five evil paths, the roads of destiny close of themselves.”

“Five evil paths” are: hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and gods. Because these five paths are the road of birth-and-death and transmigration, for a cultivator who would end birth-and-death and escape the three realms, all of them are evil paths.
“Good destinies”: here “good destinies” does not mean the three good paths among the six paths (gods, humans, and asuras), but rather the ending of the road of birth-and-death and transmigration.
“For all beings I open the Dharma-store”: teaching beings to reveal their own intrinsic nature (the Dharma-store).

“Dharma-store” is also called the store of Buddha-dharma, or the tathāgatagarbha; that is, the intrinsic nature of sentient beings, which contains and holds all the merits of the Tathāgata’s fruition-ground. (For details, see
Mind, Intrinsic Nature, and Tathāgatagarbha
Like the Buddha’s unobstructed wisdom, walking in the practice of compassion, always a teacher of gods and humans, he becomes the hero of the three realms.
Proclaiming the Dharma with the lion’s roar, delivering every sentient being, perfecting all past vows
(perfecting and fulfilling the forty-eight great vows made in the past),
all shall become Buddhas
(causing every being reborn in my land to attain Buddhahood)
“Lion’s roar”: the Buddha proclaims the Dharma without any fear, his voice shakes the ten directions, and all demons are subdued, just as when the lion roars, the hundred beasts submit.
“All shall become Buddhas”: causing every being reborn in my land to attain Buddhahood. That is, as the forty-eight vows spoken of earlier say:

“All sentient beings, including those in the realm of Yama and in the three evil paths, who come to be born in my land and receive my Dharma’s transformation, shall all accomplish anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
If this vow is fulfilled
(if this vow is about to be accomplished),
the great thousand worlds shall tremble in response
(the great thousand worlds shall tremble in resonance),
and all the gods of the sky shall rain down rare and wondrous flowers."

"The Buddha told Ānanda: when the bhikṣu Dharmākara had spoken this verse, the entire earth at once quaked in six ways. The heavens rained wondrous flowers, scattering them upon him. Music sounded of itself, and a voice in the air praised him, saying: he shall certainly attain supreme perfect enlightenment."

The Buddha told Ānanda: when the bhikṣu Dharmākara had spoken this verse, the entire earth immediately quaked in six ways. The heavens rained wondrous flowers, scattering them upon him. Music sounded of itself in the air, praising him, saying: he shall certainly attain supreme perfect enlightenment (he shall certainly become a Buddha).

“Six ways of quaking”: the six signs of auspicious quaking, namely movement, surging, quaking, striking, roaring, and bursting. These six kinds of quaking can be known and seen only by those with the divine eye; ordinary beings know nothing of them. “A voice in the air praised him, saying: he shall certainly attain supreme perfect enlightenment”: because the bhikṣu Dharmākara said in his forty-eight vows that if any one of those vows were not fulfilled, he would not attain Buddhahood. “A voice in the air praised him, saying: he shall certainly attain supreme perfect enlightenment” is a prophecy: the bhikṣu Dharmākara will certainly become a Buddha, and all forty-eight vows will be completely fulfilled.
This chapter tells how the bhikṣu Dharmākara, after cultivating through immeasurable kalpas, accumulated merit and virtue, and thereby evoked the manifestation of a Buddha-land (
“he evoked a vast and pure dwelling-place”
) — the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

“Ānanda, after the bhikṣu Dharmākara had made these vast and lofty vows before the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja, and in the midst of the assembly of gods, humans, and the great multitude, he dwelt in true wisdom, advanced with brave and vigorous effort, and single-mindedly devoted himself to adorning the wondrous land. The Buddha-land he cultivated was open and vast, surpassing and uniquely wondrous; once established, it abides forever, without decay or change.”

Ānanda, after the bhikṣu Dharmākara had made these forty-eight great vows before the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja and in the midst of the assembly of gods, humans, and the great multitude, he dwelt in true wisdom and cultivated with brave and vigorous effort, always single-mindedly devoted to cultivating and adorning the wondrous land. The Buddha-land he would cultivate was open and broad, magnificent and vast, surpassing and uniquely wondrous, altogether foremost. It abides forever just so, never decaying or growing old.

“The Buddha-land he cultivated”: the Buddha-land he cultivated was evoked and manifested by the bhikṣu Dharmākara’s immeasurable and boundless fruition-enlightenment and wondrous virtue. The Vajraśekhara Sutra says:
“This Buddha-land alone is entirely accomplished through the purity of vajra intrinsic nature.”

“Once established, it abides forever, without decay or change”: the Buddha-land he cultivated (the Land of Ultimate Bliss), once established, abides forever just so, and has no marks of decay or damage.

“For immeasurable kalpas he accumulated and planted virtuous conduct. He gave rise to no thoughts of greed, anger, delusion, or desire, and clung to nothing among forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, tactile objects, or mental objects. He delighted only in recollecting the good roots cultivated by the Buddhas of the past. He practiced the peaceful practice, far removed from falsehood. Relying on the gate of ultimate truth, he planted the roots of all virtues, counting no hardship as hardship.”

Throughout immeasurable kalpas, the bhikṣu Dharmākara accumulated and planted virtuous conduct. He gave rise to no thoughts of greed, anger, delusion, or desire, nor did he cling to the objects of the six dusts. He delighted only in recollecting the good cultivated by the Buddhas of the past. He practiced the peaceful practice, far removed from falsehood. Relying on the gate of ultimate truth, he cultivated the roots of all virtues, counting no hardship or difficulty as hardship.

“Six dusts”: the dust of form, the dust of sound, the dust of fragrance, the dust of taste, the dust of touch, and the dust of mental objects. “Dust” means defilement; it is so called because it can defile the human mind and prevent the true nature from manifesting. They are also called the six objects, being the outer objects perceived by the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind). “Ultimate truth”: the true principle of nirvāṇa’s stillness, seen by sagely wisdom, is called ultimate truth.

“With few desires and contentment, he sought only the pure Dharma, benefiting the multitude of beings. His vow and aspiration never wearied, and his power of patience was accomplished. Toward all sentient beings he always cherished compassion and patience. With a gentle countenance and loving words, he exhorted and encouraged them onward. He revered the Three Jewels and served his teachers, with no heart of falsehood or flattery.”

He had few desires and was content, seeking only good dharmas and benefiting the multitude of beings. His vow and aspiration never wearied, and his power of patience was accomplished. Toward all sentient beings he always cherished compassion and patience. With a gentle countenance and loving words, he exhorted and encouraged them onward. He revered the Three Jewels and served his teachers, with no heart of falsehood or flattery.
“Pure dharmas”: the general name for all good dharmas. “Power of patience”: the power of patient endurance. The Lotus Sutra says:
“Again I see sons of the Buddha dwelling in the power of patience; when arrogant and overbearing people revile and beat them, they can endure it all, in order to seek the Buddha-way.”
“Compassion and patience”: compassion and forbearance. “Exhorted”: admonished and instructed. “Encouraged them onward”: urged them to advance.

“Adorning all practices, his model and demeanor were complete. He contemplated all dharmas as illusory, and his samādhi was ever still. He guarded well the karma of speech, never ridiculing the faults of others; he guarded well the karma of body, never transgressing the precepts and deportment; he guarded well the karma of mind, pure and undefiled. Toward all cities, towns, kinsmen, and treasures, he had no attachment whatsoever. Always with giving, precepts, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom — the practices of the six pāramitās — he taught and established beings, causing them to dwell in the supreme and true way.”

The bhikṣu Dharmākara adorned all practices, and his model and demeanor were complete. He contemplated all dharmas as illusory, and his samādhi was ever still. He guarded well the karma of speech, never ridiculing the faults of others; he guarded well the karma of body, never transgressing the precepts and deportment; he guarded well the karma of mind, pure and undefiled. Toward all cities, towns, kinsmen, and treasures, he had no attachment whatsoever. Always with the wondrous practices of the six pāramitās — giving, precepts, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom — he taught and established beings, causing them to dwell in the supreme and true way.

“Model and demeanor”: the standard that conduct should follow. “Contemplated all dharmas as illusory”: seeing all dharmas as like illusions. “Precepts and deportment”: precepts are the moral rules, deportment is the proper bearing; these are what a cultivator must follow in conducting himself in the world.

“Because he accomplished such good roots, wherever he was born, immeasurable treasures naturally appeared in response. Sometimes he was a householder or a man of wealth, of noble or honored family; sometimes a kṣatriya king or a wheel-turning sage emperor; sometimes a lord of the six heavens of desire, or even a Brahmā king. Before all Buddhas he reverently made offerings, never interrupting. Such merit cannot be fully told.”

Because the bhikṣu Dharmākara had accomplished such good roots, wherever he was born, immeasurable treasures naturally welled up. In his successive lives he was sometimes a householder or a man of wealth, of noble or honored family; sometimes a kṣatriya king or a wheel-turning sage king; sometimes the lord of the heavens of the desire realm, or even the great Brahmā king of the form realm. Before all Buddhas he reverently made offerings, never interrupting. Such merit cannot be fully told.

“Immeasurable treasures naturally appeared in response”: because the bhikṣu Dharmākara accumulated over many kalpas the merit of giving and keeping precepts, treasures appeared in response and welled up of themselves. “Householder”: a general term for one who accumulates wealth and possesses virtue. “Kṣatriya”: that is, kṣatriya, the second of India’s four castes. “Four castes”: brahmins, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras. Brahmins were the priests of ancient India, holding the highest authority; kṣatriyas were the royal class, honored equally with the brahmins; vaiśyas were the ordinary class of workers, farmers, and merchants; śūdras were slaves made to serve others. “Six heavens of desire”: the desire realm (the world inhabited by beings who have the two desires of sexuality and food) has six levels of heaven, hence the name six heavens of desire: the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Heaven of Enjoying Transformations, and the Heaven of Freely Enjoying Others’ Transformations. “Lord of the six heavens of desire”: the lord of each heaven of the desire realm. “Brahmā king”: short for the great Brahmā king. “Form realm”: above the desire realm; because the beings of this realm have only material bodies and are free from the two desires of sexuality and food, it is called the form realm.

“Sometimes the lord of the heavens of the desire realm, or even the great Brahmā king of the form realm”: the Sutra of the Great Vehicle of Immeasurable Life, Spoken by the Buddha (Song translation) says:
“Ānanda, when the bhikṣu who made the vows
(the bhikṣu Dharmākara),

while practicing the bodhisattva path, was before all Buddhas, he was reverent and respectful. He served and made offerings without ever interrupting. As a king of the Four Great Kings, he constantly came before the Buddhas, reverently bowing and making offerings. As a lord of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, he constantly came before the Buddhas, reverently bowing and making offerings. As a lord of the Yāma Heaven, a lord of the Tuṣita Heaven, a lord of the Heaven of Enjoying Transformations, a lord of the Heaven of Freely Enjoying Others’ Transformations, and even as a great Brahmā king, he constantly came before the Buddhas, reverently bowing and making offerings. ”
“From his body and mouth there constantly came immeasurable wondrous fragrance, like that of candana
(zhān)

and utpala flowers, and its fragrance pervaded immeasurable worlds. Wherever he was born, his form was dignified, and the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary marks were all complete. From his hands there constantly came endless treasures and adornments, everything needed, the finest of things, bringing benefit and joy to sentient beings. By this cause and condition, he could cause immeasurable beings to give rise to the aspiration for anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

Through the response evoked by his merit, from the bhikṣu Dharmākara’s body and mouth there constantly came immeasurable wondrous fragrance, like that of candana and utpala flowers, and its fragrance pervaded immeasurable worlds. Wherever he was born, his form was dignified, and the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary marks were all complete. From his hands there constantly came endless treasures and adornments, everything needed, the finest of things, to bring benefit and joy to sentient beings. By this cause and condition, he could cause immeasurable beings to give rise to the aspiration for anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.

“Eighty secondary marks” is also called the eighty follow-the-form marks, namely: an invisible crown of the head; a high nose with unseen nostrils; eyebrows like the new moon; earlobes hanging low; a body firm as Nārāyaṇa’s; joints like hooked chains; a body that turns at once like an elephant king; feet that leave prints four inches above the ground when walking; nails the color of red copper, thin and glossy; knee bones firm and perfectly round; a clean body; a soft body; an unbent body; round and slender fingers; hidden and covered finger-lines; deep and unseen veins; unseen ankles; a glossy body; a body that holds itself without bending; a fulfilled body; complete bearing and deportment; a full and perfect bearing; an abode so secure that none can move him; majesty that overawes all; all beings rejoicing at the sight of him; a face neither long nor large; proper features with an unyielding countenance; a full and perfect face and eyes; lips the color of the bimba fruit; a voice deep and far-reaching; a navel deep and perfectly round; hairs curling to the right; fulfilled hands and feet; hands and feet that follow his intent; clear and straight hand-lines; long hand-lines; unbroken hand-lines; all beings of evil mind becoming gentle and joyful at the sight of him; a broad and exceedingly lovely face; a face as pure and full as the moon; speaking gently and joyfully according to the minds of beings; fragrance issuing from his pores; supreme fragrance issuing from his mouth; a bearing like the lion’s; advancing and resting like an elephant king; a gait like the goose king’s; a head like the mādhava fruit; a voice complete in every part; four teeth white and sharp; a red tongue; a thin tongue; red hairs; soft and clean hairs; broad and long eyes; the marks of the gate of death complete; hands and feet red and white like the color of lotus flowers; an unseen navel; an unseen belly; a slender belly; a body that does not lean or move; a body that bears weight; a large body; a tall body; hands and feet soft, clean, smooth, and glossy; a halo extending ten feet on all four sides; light shining as he walks; looking upon beings with impartiality; never slighting beings; voice that neither increases nor decreases with the voices of beings; teaching the Dharma without attachment; teaching the Dharma according to the language of beings; a voice that responds to beings; teaching the Dharma in sequence according to causes and conditions; all beings finding his marks inexhaustible to behold; beholding him without ever being satiated; long and lovely hair; hair never disheveled; hair curled in a lovely whorl; hair the color of blue pearls; hands and feet bearing the marks of virtue.

“The Buddha told Ānanda: the bhikṣu Dharmākara cultivated the bodhisattva path, accumulating merit and virtue beyond measure or bound. In all dharmas he attained freedom, which is not something that verbal discrimination can know. The vows he made were perfectly accomplished, and he truly abides in a pure Buddha-land complete in adornment, majestic in virtue, vast and great.”

The Buddha told Ānanda: the bhikṣu Dharmākara cultivated the bodhisattva path, accumulating merit and virtue beyond measure or bound. In all dharmas he attained freedom; this is not something that verbal discrimination can know. The forty-eight great vows he made were perfectly accomplished, and he truly abides in a pure Buddha-land complete in adornment, majestic in virtue, vast and great.

“When Ānanda heard what the Buddha said, he addressed the World-Honored One: the Bodhisattva Dharmākara who attained bodhi — is he a Buddha of the past? A Buddha of the future? Or a present Buddha now dwelling in another world?”

When Ānanda heard what the Buddha said, he addressed the World-Honored One: the Bodhisattva Dharmākara who attained Buddhahood — is he a Buddha of the past? A Buddha of the future? Or a present Buddha dwelling in another world?

“The World-Honored One told him: that Buddha Tathāgata, in coming has nowhere he comes from, in going has nowhere he goes; he is neither born nor extinguished, and is not past, present, or future. But to repay his vows and save beings, he now appears in the west, ten billion Buddha-lands from here, in a world named Ultimate Bliss. Dharmākara became a Buddha, with the name Amitābha. Ten kalpas have passed since his attainment of Buddhahood. He now teaches the Dharma, surrounded with reverence by immeasurable and countless multitudes of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.”

The World-Honored One told Ānanda: that Buddha Tathāgata (Amitābha Buddha), in coming has nowhere he comes from, in going has nowhere he goes; he is neither born nor extinguished, and is neither a Buddha of the past, nor a Buddha of the present, nor a Buddha of the future. But to repay his vows and broadly save beings,
he now appears in the west, ten billion Buddha-lands from here,

in a world named Ultimate Bliss. Dharmākara became a Buddha, with the name Amitābha. Ten kalpas have passed since his attainment of Buddhahood. He now teaches the Dharma, surrounded with reverence by immeasurable and countless multitudes of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.

“That Buddha Tathāgata, in coming has nowhere he comes from, in going has nowhere he goes; he is neither born nor extinguished, and is not past, present, or future”: this is the ultimate truth, spoken with respect to the true mark of all dharmas.
“He now appears in the west, ten billion Buddha-lands from here”: the assembled Sutra of Immeasurable Life Tathāgata (Tang translation) says:

“The Buddha told Ānanda: to the west of here, ten billion Buddha-lands away, there is a world named Ultimate Bliss. The bhikṣu Dharmākara attained Buddhahood there, with the name Immeasurable Life, and now teaches the Dharma.”
The Amitābha Sutra Spoken by the Buddha says:

“The Buddha told the elder Śāriputra: passing from here to the west through ten billion Buddha-lands, there is a world named Ultimate Bliss. In that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha, who now teaches the Dharma.”
“Ten kalpas have passed since his attainment of Buddhahood”: the Sutra of Immeasurable Life (Wei translation) says:

“Ānanda asked the Buddha: did the Bodhisattva Dharmākara already become a Buddha and then enter extinction? Or has he not yet become a Buddha? Or is he now present? The Buddha told Ānanda: the Bodhisattva Dharmākara has now become a Buddha; he is present in the west, ten billion lands from here, and his Buddha-world is named Peace and Bliss. Ānanda asked again: how long has it been since that Buddha attained the way? The Buddha said: since his attainment of Buddhahood, ten kalpas have passed.”
The Amitābha Sutra Spoken by the Buddha says:
“Ten kalpas have passed since Amitābha Buddha attained Buddhahood.”

“The Buddha told how Amitābha Buddha, while a bodhisattva, sought and attained these vows.
