[The fasts and precepts] Cleansing the impurities of one's own mind is called “the fast”; prohibiting the faults of one's own conduct is called “the precepts.” The fasts and precepts mean keeping the precepts so as to cut off all craving and all faults. [Zeng (
zēng
)] The general term in ancient times for silk fabrics. [Hanging silk banners] Hanging banners made of colored silk in the Buddha halls.
[Those of the lowest grade, even if unable to perform all these merits and virtues,
should give rise to the mind of supreme bodhi and single-mindedly and exclusively recite Amitābha Buddha

. They rejoice, believe, and delight, and give rise to no doubt. With the utmost sincere mind they vow to be born in that land. When such a person is about to die, he dreams of that Buddha and likewise attains rebirth. His merit, virtue, and wisdom are next to those of the middle grade.]

Those of the lowest grade (the lowest class): even if unable to perform all the merits and virtues described above, they should give rise to the mind of supreme bodhi and single-mindedly and exclusively recite Amitābha Buddha. They rejoice, believe, and delight, and give rise to no doubt. With the utmost sincere mind they vow to be born in the Western land of Ultimate Bliss. When such a person is about to die, he dreams of Amitābha Buddha and likewise attains rebirth in the Western land of Ultimate Bliss. His merit, virtue, and wisdom are next to those of the middle grade.
The above three grades are those who practice the Pure Land exclusively; what follows explains those who do not practice the Pure Land exclusively.

[If there are sentient beings who dwell in the Great Vehicle, and with a pure mind turn toward Amitāyus, even to ten thoughts, vowing to be born in his land; and those who hear this profound Dharma and at once give rise to faith and understanding, even to obtaining a single thought of pure mind and, with that single thought, recollect that Buddha — such a person, at the time of death, as though in a dream, sees Amitābha Buddha and will certainly be born in that land, gaining non-retrogression and supreme bodhi.]

If there are sentient beings who dwell in the Great Vehicle and, with a pure mind (undefiled by deluded thoughts), invoke Amitābha Buddha, even to ten recitations at the point of death, vowing to be born in the Western land of Ultimate Bliss; and again, if there are sentient beings who hear the Pure Land Dharma-gate and at once give rise to faith and understanding, even to obtaining a single thought of pure mind and with that single thought invoking Amitābha Buddha — these two kinds of people, at the time of death, as though in a dream, see Amitābha Buddha and will certainly be born in the Western land of Ultimate Bliss, gaining the stage of non-retrogression and reaching Buddhahood.

[Moreover, Ānanda, if good men or good women hear this scripture, receive, uphold, read, and recite it, copy and make offerings to it, continuing day and night, and seek birth in that land; give rise to the bodhi mind, uphold all the precepts, firmly keeping them without violation; benefit sentient beings and give to them all the good roots they have made, bringing them peace and joy; and recollect Amitābha Buddha and his land — such a person, at the end of life, with the Buddha's form and marks and all manner of adornment, is born in the jeweled land, quickly hears the Dharma, and never falls back.]

Moreover, Ānanda, if good men or good women hear this scripture, receive, uphold, read, and recite it, copy and make offerings to it, and day and night without interruption seek birth in the Western land of Ultimate Bliss; give rise to the bodhi mind, uphold all the precepts, firmly keeping them without violation; benefit sentient beings and give to them all the good roots they have made, bringing them peace and joy; and recollect Amitābha Buddha and the land of Ultimate Bliss — such a person, at the end of life, with the Buddha's form and marks and all manner of adornment, is born in the jeweled land, quickly hears the Dharma, and never falls back.

[The precepts] Prohibiting the non-precept and guarding against evil. The precepts laid down by the Buddha are variously divided into the five precepts, the eight precepts, the śrāmaṇera precepts, and the full precepts. [With the Buddha's form and marks] Their form and marks are like the Buddha's — a body of true golden hue with the thirty-two marks.

[Moreover, Ānanda, if sentient beings wish to be born in that land, though they cannot greatly practice vigor and meditative concentration and fully uphold the sutras and precepts, they should at least do good. That is: first, not to kill; second, not to steal; third, not to commit sexual misconduct; fourth, not to speak falsely; fifth, not to speak frivolously; sixth, not to speak harshly; seventh, not to speak duplicitously; eighth, not to be greedy; ninth, not to be angry; tenth, not to be deluded. Thus, day and night they reflect upon the manifold merits and virtues and manifold adornments of Amitābha Buddha in the land of Ultimate Bliss. With single-minded hearts they take refuge, bow in homage, and make offerings. When such a person is about to die, without alarm or fear, with a mind not confused, he attains rebirth in that Buddha's land.]

Moreover, Ānanda, if sentient beings wish to be born in that land, though they cannot greatly practice vigor and meditative concentration and fully uphold the sutras and precepts, they should at least do good. That is: first, not to kill; second, not to steal; third, not to commit sexual misconduct; fourth, not to speak falsely (not to speak words that are false and untrue); fifth, not to speak frivolously (not to speak filthy words, meaningless words, or words containing lewd intent); sixth, not to speak harshly (not to revile or mock others with vicious words); seventh, not to speak duplicitously (not to stir up trouble and set others at variance); eighth, not to be greedy; ninth, not to be angry; tenth, not to be deluded (not to be foolish). Thus, day and night they reflect upon the manifold merits and virtues and manifold adornments of Amitābha Buddha in the land of Ultimate Bliss. With single-minded hearts they take refuge, bow in homage, and make offerings. When such a person is about to die, without alarm or fear, with a mind not confused, he attains rebirth in that Buddha's land.

[If one has many affairs and cannot leave the household, and has no leisure to greatly cultivate the fasts and precepts and keep a single pure mind. When one has free time, rectify body and mind, cut off desire and put away anxiety, and with a compassionate mind be diligent. One should not be angry or envious, and must not be gluttonous
tiè
or stingy
qiān
and grudging. One must not later regret, nor be of two minds.]

If one's affairs are many and one cannot leave the household, and has no leisure to greatly cultivate the fasts and precepts and keep a single pure mind, then whenever one has free time, one should rectify body and mind, cut off desire and put away anxiety, and with a compassionate mind be diligent. One should not be angry or envious, and must not be gluttonous or stingy. Toward the Pure Land Dharma-gate one must not later regret, nor be of two minds.
[No leisure] To have no time; to be unable to manage it. [Gluttonous (tiè)] Insatiably greedy. [Later regret] Faith that is not firm, believing first and doubting afterward.

[One should be filial and obedient, sincere, loyal, and trustworthy. One should believe that the words of the Buddhist scriptures are profound, and believe that doing good brings blessings. Uphold and keep such teachings without fail. Reflect and ponder deeply, wishing to attain liberation. Day and night constantly recollect, wishing to be born in Amitābha Buddha's pure Buddha-land. Those who for ten days and ten nights, or even one day and one night, do not break off, at the end of life all attain rebirth in that land and practice the bodhisattva path.]

One should be filial and obedient, sincere, loyal, and trustworthy. One should believe that the words of the Buddhist scriptures are profound, and believe that doing good brings blessings. Uphold and keep such teachings without fail. Reflect and ponder deeply, wishing to attain liberation (to escape the round of rebirth). Day and night constantly recollect, wishing to be born in Amitābha Buddha's pure Buddha-land. Those who for ten days and ten nights, or even one day and one night, do not break off, at the end of life all attain rebirth in that land and practice the bodhisattva path.

[All those reborn there attain non-retrogression, are all endowed with the thirty-two marks of golden hue, and will all become Buddhas. In whatever direction's Buddha-land they wish to become Buddhas, it is according to the wish of their hearts. According to their diligence, sooner or later, seeking the Way without rest, they will certainly attain it, and will not lose what they have vowed.]

All those reborn there attain the stage of non-retrogression, are all endowed with the thirty-two marks of golden hue, and will all become Buddhas. In whatever direction's Buddha-land they wish to become Buddhas, it is entirely according to the wish of their hearts. According to their diligence, sooner or later, seeking the Way without rest, they will certainly become Buddhas, and will not lose what they have vowed.
[Ānanda, because of this benefit of meaning, the Tathāgatas of immeasurable, countless, inconceivable, unequaled, boundless worlds all together praise all the merit and virtue of Amitāyus Buddha.]
Ānanda, because of this benefit of meaning, the Tathāgatas of the immeasurable, countless, inconceivable, unequaled, boundless worlds all together praise all the merit and virtue of Amitābha Buddha.
[Benefit of meaning] “Meaning” is just and fitting principle and conduct; “benefit” is benefit and advantage.

blocks.text: 26. Paying Homage, Making Offerings, and Hearing the Dharma

inline.s: [Moreover, Ānanda, the assemblies of bodhisattvas of the worlds of the ten directions, wishing to behold and worship Amitāyus Buddha of the land of Ultimate Bliss, each with fragrant flowers, banners, and jeweled canopies, proceed to where the Buddha is. Reverently making offerings, they listen to and receive the sutras and Dharma, proclaim and spread the teaching, and praise the merit, virtue, and adornments of that Buddha-land.]

Moreover, Ānanda, the assemblies of bodhisattvas of the worlds of the ten directions, wishing to behold and worship Amitābha Buddha of the land of Ultimate Bliss, each with fragrant flowers, banners, and jeweled canopies, go to where Amitābha Buddha is. Reverently making offerings, they hear and receive the sutras and Dharma spoken by Amitābha Buddha, and again proclaim and spread his teaching throughout the ten directions, praising the merit and adornments of the land of Ultimate Bliss.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
At that time the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
In the eastern Buddha-lands, numerous as Ganges-sands, bodhisattvas, countless as those sands, come to pay homage to Amitāyus.
South, West, North, and the four intermediate directions
— that is, the south, west, and north, together with the southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast —
and so too above and below
— and likewise for the zenith and the nadir —
they all, with
the utmost reverence,
present offerings of rare and wondrous treasures.
They
pour forth harmonious and elegant music, singing in praise of the Supremely Honored One
— that is, in praise of Amitābha Buddha —
and penetrating to the uttermost the powers and wisdom of the spiritual penetrations
— the spiritual penetrations and wisdom fully mastered —
they roam freely into the profound Dharma-gate.

[The Supremely Honored One] The most exalted among all honored ones; this is an honorific title for a Buddha. [Roam freely into the profound Dharma-gate] The bodhisattvas, in their songs of praise, extol Amitābha Buddha as having exhausted the very source of the true character of all dharmas; freely and without obstruction they roam through this most profound Dharma-gate.
Hearing the Buddha's holy name of virtue, they gain peace and great benefit; among all kinds of offerings, they cultivate diligently, never weary or slack.
They contemplate that surpassing land
— the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss —

so subtle and wondrous as to defy thought; its merits universally adorn it, and the Buddha-lands of all Buddhas cannot compare. Therefore they bring forth the unsurpassed mind and vow swiftly to attain bodhi.
The foregoing is the offering, singing, praise, and aspiration of the bodhisattvas from the worlds of the ten directions who come to pay homage to Amitābha Buddha.
At that moment the Immeasurable Honored One
— that is, Amitābha Buddha —

smiles and reveals his golden countenance. Light issues from his mouth and shines throughout the lands of the ten directions; the light returns, circles the Buddha, and after three circuits enters at the crown of his head.
Seeing this light, the bodhisattvas at once attain the stage of non-retrogression; the whole assembly then
— that is, all the great multitude present at the assembly —
rejoice together and congratulate one another.
What follows is Amitābha Buddha's teaching.
The Buddha's words, like pealing thunder
— Amitābha Buddha teaches in the Brahma voice, pure and wondrous; like a thunderclap, it startles the whole assembly into sudden awakening.
In eight-toned voice he pours forth the wondrous sound.

[Brahma voice] The pure and clear sound uttered by the great Brahma king; the Buddha's voice is likewise, and so among the thirty-two marks there is the mark of the Brahma voice: “the Brahma voice, clear and far-reaching.” The Lotus Sutra says:
“The Brahma voice is subtle and wondrous, delighting all who hear it.”

[The eight-toned voice] The eight kinds of sound unique to a Buddha: first, the supremely excellent voice — no sound of the world or beyond the world can compare with it; second, the soft voice — the Buddha's voice is soft, and those who hear it rejoice; third, the harmonious voice — it harmonizes the minds of beings and causes them to remove afflictions; fourth, the infallible voice — the Buddha's wisdom is perfect and bright, and all who hear the sound he utters gain right views; fifth, the not-feminine voice — the Buddha's voice is complete in the four fearlessnesses, so that hearers are convinced; sixth, the honored-wisdom voice — hearing the Buddha's voice, beings give rise to reverence and awaken wisdom; seventh, the far-reaching voice — near at hand the Buddha's voice is not loud, heard from afar it is not faint, and there is no distance it does not reach (however far away, there is nowhere it does not arrive); eighth, the inexhaustible voice — the Buddha's voice flows on endlessly, its resonance never ceasing.
The true followers who come from the ten directions
— the bodhisattvas who come from the worlds of the ten directions —
I know all their vows
— I know completely their surpassing great vows —
they aspire to adorn the pure lands
— they resolve to take in and adorn pure and serene Buddha-lands —
and receiving the prediction, they shall become Buddhas.
[Receiving the prediction]
Receiving from a Buddha the assurance that one will in future surely become a Buddha.
They
awaken to all dharmas as like a dream, an illusion, an echo
— that is, they enter the true character of all dharmas and awaken to the truth that every dharma is ultimately empty, nothing whatsoever, unobtainable —
and fulfilling all their wondrous vows
— fulfilling their surpassing great vows
— they shall surely accomplish such a land
— they will certainly build just such a Buddha-land —
They
know the land to be like an image or a shadow
— they understand that the Buddha-land too is an illusion —
and ever bring forth the heart of vast vows, consummating the bodhisattva path
— thoroughly and perfectly cultivating the bodhisattva path —
complete in the sources of all merit, they cultivate the supreme bodhi practice
— they cultivate the surpassing practice of bodhi —
and receiving the prediction, they shall become Buddhas.

[Knowing the land to be like an image or a shadow] They understand that the Buddha-land too is like the image of a thing: though it arises from a real substance, it has no real nature. This speaks of how the bodhisattvas enter the true character of all dharmas and understand that the Buddha-land is likewise an illusion. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

“Perfect enlightenment shines universally, in still quiescence without duality; within it, the hundreds of thousands of millions of asaṃkhyeyas of inexpressible Ganges-sands of Buddha-worlds are like flowers in the sky, arising and perishing in confusion.”
(For the notes, see, in detail,
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, Explained
They
thoroughly understand the nature of all dharmas
— they thoroughly understand the true character of all dharmas —
that all is empty and without self
— the myriad phenomena are all illusions and have no real substance; for details, see
The True Character of All Dharmas.
And single-mindedly seek the pure Buddha-land; they shall surely accomplish such a land,
they will certainly build just such a Buddha-land.

Hearing the Dharma, they delight in receiving and practicing it; they reach the pure place, and before the Immeasurable Honored One they shall surely receive the prediction and attain equal enlightenment.

[Before the Immeasurable Honored One they shall surely receive the prediction and attain equal enlightenment] They will surely receive from Amitābha Buddha the prediction that they shall become Buddhas. Here “equal enlightenment” is an abbreviation of “perfect equal enlightenment.”

The following passage says: the bodhisattvas present at the assembly wish to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and bring forth great vows, so that in the future when they themselves become Buddhas, their Buddha-lands will likewise be just like the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. They will universally deliver all beings from the six paths of rebirth and bring them to be reborn in their own Buddha-lands.
The land of boundless surpassing glory
— boundless and immeasurable, and exceeding all the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, it is the Land of Ultimate Bliss —
owes all to that Buddha's power of original vows
— precisely through the power of Amitābha Buddha's surpassing original vows —
and those who hear the Name and wish for rebirth
— the bodhisattvas, hearing the Name of Amitābha Buddha, wish to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss —
attain of themselves the stage of non-retrogression,
having arrived there, they themselves attain the stage of non-retrogression.
The bodhisattvas bring forth their highest vows
— the bodhisattvas bring forth the most vast of vows —
, vowing that their own lands shall be without difference
— vowing that the Buddha-lands they shall build in the future will be just like the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss —
and, with universal mindfulness
— with equal great compassion —
deliver all
— delivering every living being —
; they
— that is, those beings —
all bring forth the bodhi mind, abandon the body of rebirth, and together reach the other shore
— all are reborn in those Buddha-lands of the bodhisattvas, which are like the Land of Ultimate Bliss; this is the other shore where there is no birth and death, no rebirth —
[Vowing that their own lands shall be without difference] They vow that the Buddha-lands they themselves build shall be just like the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
This is the same as Prince Ajātaśatru and the five hundred great elders earlier in the text, who in their hearts made this vow: when we become Buddhas, may we be just like Amitābha Buddha.
The Sutra of Immeasurable Life as Spoken by the Buddha (the Wei translation) says:

“The bodhisattvas bring forth their highest vows, vowing that their own lands shall be without difference; with universal mindfulness they deliver all, and their fame shines throughout the ten directions.”

The phrase in the sutra, “with universal mindfulness they deliver all,” clearly means that the bodhisattvas who bring forth the highest vows wish to deliver all living beings, bringing them to the Buddha-lands they shall build in the future, which are like the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. [Abandon the body of rebirth] “Those” refers to the beings whom these bodhisattvas are to deliver, not to the bodhisattvas themselves. For the bodhisattvas who are able to come from Buddha-lands of the ten directions to pay homage and make offerings to Amitābha Buddha no longer have a body of rebirth.

blocks.text: Singing Praise of the Buddha's Virtues, 27

inline.s: The following passage tells of how the bodhisattvas of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss fly and transform themselves to the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, and of the concrete circumstances of their making offerings to all the Buddhas.

[The Buddha said to Ānanda: The bodhisattvas in that land, by the Buddha's awesome spiritual power, within the time of a single meal go again to the boundless pure lands of the ten directions and make offerings to all the Buddhas. Flowers, incense, banners, and canopies — the implements of offering — arrive as soon as they are thought of, and all appear in their hands. Rare, wondrous, and surpassing, they are not such as the world possesses. These they present to all the Buddhas and to the assemblies of bodhisattvas.]

The Buddha said to Ānanda: The bodhisattvas of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, by the Buddha's awesome spiritual power, within the time of a single meal go to the boundless pure lands of the ten directions and make offerings to all the Buddhas. Fresh flowers, precious incense, banners, canopies, and other implements of offering arrive as soon as they are thought of, and all appear in their hands. Rare, wondrous, and surpassing, they are not such as the world possesses. They are used to make offerings to all the Buddhas of the boundless pure lands of the ten directions and to the assemblies of bodhisattvas.
[The time of a single meal] The time it takes to eat one meal. The Perfection of Wisdom Sutra,
fascicle three hundred forty-seven,

the Entrustment Chapter, divides time by length in order as follows: a full day and night, one day, half a day, one shi (equivalent to two hours today), the time of a meal, a moment, an instant, and a flash.

[The flowers they scatter there at once join together in the air into a single flower. The flowers all face downward and form a perfectly round and complete canopy. In a hundred thousand hues of light, each hue with its own fragrance, the fragrance pervades everywhere. The smallest of these canopies fills ten yojanas, and so it doubles again and again, until it covers three thousand great thousand worlds. According to their sequence, they dissolve one after another. If new flowers are not scattered again, the flowers scattered before never fall. In the midst of the air they play celestial music together, and with subtle and wondrous sounds sing praise of the Buddha's virtues.]

The fresh flowers they scatter at once join together in the air into a single flower. The flowers all face downward, their edges perfectly round and complete, and they transform into a canopy, giving forth a hundred thousand hues of light. Each hue of light again sends out a different fragrance, which pervades the four directions. The smallest of the canopies is fully ten yojanas across, and so it doubles again and again, until it covers three thousand great thousand worlds. According to their sequence, they dissolve one after another. If new flowers are not scattered again, the fresh flowers scattered before remain suspended in the air. In the midst of the air they play celestial music together, and with subtle and wondrous sounds sing praise of the Buddha's virtues.

[In but a moment they return to their own land and all assemble in the seven-jeweled lecture hall. The Buddha Immeasurable Life then broadly proclaims the great teaching for them and expounds the wondrous Dharma without restraint. There is none who is not filled with joy, their minds understanding and attaining the Way.]

In but a moment they return to the Land of Ultimate Bliss and all assemble in the seven-jeweled lecture hall. Amitābha Buddha then broadly proclaims the great teaching for them and expounds the wondrous Dharma thoroughly. There is none in the assembly who is not filled with joy, their minds understanding and attaining the Way.

[At that very time a fragrant breeze blows upon the seven-jeweled trees and brings forth the five tones. Countless wondrous flowers scatter in every direction with the wind, making offerings of themselves, and so it continues without cease. All the celestial beings bring

hundreds of thousands of flowers and fragrances and ten thousand kinds of music and dance, and make offerings to that Buddha and to the assemblies of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas. Coming and going, back and forth, they are joyful and happy. All this is through the added power of Amitābha Buddha's original vows, and because those beings once made offerings to the Tathāgatas, so that their roots of virtue continue without diminution, because they cultivated well, because they gathered well, and because they accomplished well.]

At that very time a fragrant breeze blows upon the seven-jeweled trees, bringing forth the five tones (gong, shang, jue, zhi, and yu). Countless wondrous flowers scatter in every direction with the wind, making offerings of themselves, and so it continues without cease. All the celestial beings of the heavens bring hundreds of thousands of fresh flowers and precious fragrances and ten thousand kinds of music and dance (music and dancing), and make offerings to Amitābha Buddha and to the great assemblies of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas. Coming and going, back and forth, they are joyful (delighted) and happy. All this is through the added power of Amitābha Buddha's original vows, and because they (all the celestial beings) once made offerings to the Tathāgatas, so that their roots of virtue continue without diminution, because they cultivated well, because they gathered well, and because they accomplished well.
[To bring
jī
] To carry along.

[The Buddha said to Ānanda: All the bodhisattvas in that Buddha-land clearly see and clearly hear the affairs of the eight directions, above and below, and of past, future, and present. The celestial beings and human beings, and even the flying and wriggling creatures — the good and evil of their minds, what their mouths wish to say, when they will be delivered, and when they will attain the Way and be reborn there — they know all beforehand.]

The Buddha said to Ānanda: All the bodhisattvas of the Land of Ultimate Bliss can clearly see and clearly hear the affairs of the eight directions, above and below (the ten directions), and of past, future, and present. As for beings from the celestial beings and human beings above down to the flying and wriggling creatures — the good and evil of their minds, what their mouths wish to say, when they will be delivered, and when they will attain the Way and be reborn there — they all know beforehand.

[Again, the śrāvakas in that Buddha-land have a bodily radiance of one xun, while the radiance of the bodhisattvas shines for a hundred yojanas. There are two bodhisattvas, foremost and most honored, whose awesome spiritual radiance universally illumines three thousand great thousand worlds.]

Again, in the Land of Ultimate Bliss the śrāvakas have a bodily radiance of eight chi, while the radiance of the bodhisattvas shines for a hundred yojanas. There are two bodhisattvas, foremost and most honored, whose awesome spiritual radiance universally illumines three thousand great thousand worlds.
[Xun] An ancient unit of length; one xun equals eight chi.
[Ānanda said to the Buddha: What are the names of those two bodhisattvas?]
Ānanda said to the Buddha: What are the names of those two bodhisattvas?

[The Buddha said: One is named Avalokiteśvara, and one is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta. These two bodhisattvas cultivate the bodhisattva practice in the Sahā world, and are reborn in that land, where they constantly attend upon Amitābha Buddha, one to his left and one to his right. If they wish to go to the places of the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions, they arrive as they wish. They now dwell in this world and bring great benefit and happiness. Should good men and good women in the world meet with urgent danger and terror, let them simply take refuge in Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, and there is none who will not be freed.]

The Buddha said: One is named Avalokiteśvara, and one is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta. These two bodhisattvas cultivate the bodhisattva practice in the Sahā world and are reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, where they constantly attend upon Amitābha Buddha, one to his left and one to his right. If they wish to go to the places of the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions, they arrive as they wish. They now dwell in this Sahā world and bring great benefit and happiness (rescuing from danger, removing suffering, and bestowing joy) upon all beings. Should good men and good women in the world meet with urgent danger and terror, let them simply take refuge in Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, and there is none who will not be freed.

[Vast and profound vow-power] The vow-power of the bodhisattvas of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, by which they benefit themselves and transform others, is vast and profound. [Benefiting themselves and transforming others] While cultivating their own practice, they also deliver others.

[Again, Ānanda, all the bodhisattvas in that Buddha-land, whether present or future, shall ultimately reach the stage of one remaining lifetime. The only exception is those of great vows, who enter the realms of birth and death to deliver the multitude of beings. They utter the lion's roar, put on
huàn
the great armor,

and adorn themselves with the merit of their vast vows. Though born into the evil world of the five turbidities, they appear just like those beings, yet until they attain Buddhahood they never fall into the evil paths; and wherever they are born, they always know their former lives.

Again, Ānanda: all the bodhisattvas in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, whether present or future, will ultimately reach the stage of one remaining lifetime (that is, the equal-enlightenment bodhisattva). The only exception is those bodhisattvas who make surpassing great vows: they willingly take birth in the impure lands of birth and death to deliver the beings there. Like the Buddha himself they expound the Dharma (that is, they utter the lion's roar), spreading the Pure Land Dharma-gate and delivering beings to rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Clad in the great armor adorned with the merit of their vast vows, though born into the evil world of the five turbidities and appearing as one of that kind, they never fall into the evil paths until they attain Buddhahood; and wherever they are born, they are free of the delusion of the intervening skandha and know everything of their former lives.

[Enter the realms of birth and death] To take birth in an impure land of birth and death and rebirth. [The lion's roar] The Buddha's proclamation of the Dharma amid the great assembly, fearing no band of the heterodox or of other teachings, is like the lion's roar that overawes a hundred beasts. [Utter the lion's roar] To expound the Dharma just as the Buddha does. [The delusion of the intervening skandha] That whereby one forgets as soon as one is reborn in another body.

[Amitābha Buddha wishes to deliver all classes of beings in the worlds of the ten directions, causing them all to be reborn in his land and all to attain the path of nirvāṇa; and those who are bodhisattvas he causes all to become Buddhas. And once they have become Buddhas, they in turn teach and deliver one another. Thus it continues, turning and turning, beyond all reckoning.]

Amitābha Buddha wishes to deliver all classes of beings in the worlds of the ten directions, causing them all to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and to attain the path to Buddhahood; and those beings who are already bodhisattvas he causes to become Buddhas. Once they have become Buddhas, they in turn teach the Pure Land Dharma-gate throughout the worlds of the ten directions, and in turn deliver the beings there to rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Thus, teaching and delivering one another in turn, they are beyond all counting.
[Nirvāṇa (
huán
)] That is, nirvāṇa.

[Amitābha Buddha wishes to deliver all classes of beings in the worlds of the ten directions, causing them all to be reborn in his land (the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss)] This is Amitābha Buddha’s measureless compassion. It is because Amitābha Buddha, while still on the causal ground, endured hardship through measureless, inconceivable, countless kalpas that the matchlessly surpassing Western Land of Ultimate Bliss was brought to completion, and so the Pure Land Dharma-gate came to be. Beings of the evil world of the five turbidities who cultivate the Pure Land Dharma-gate need only, at the end of life, recite the name of Amitābha Buddha ten times in continuous succession, and they at once attain rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, ending birth and death and escaping rebirth (for details, see
The Conditions for Rebirth

), whereas other Dharma-gates require utterly cutting off afflictions (the delusions of view and thought) before one can end birth and death and escape rebirth. Comparing the difficulty of the two: the former is like hoisting sail before a favorable wind, the latter like an ant climbing a high mountain. Thus it is said:
“In the Dharma-ending age, countless millions cultivate, yet hardly one attains the Way; only by relying on Buddha-recitation does one transcend birth and death.”
[And other Dharma-gates require utterly cutting off afflictions (the delusions of view and thought) before one can end birth and death and escape rebirth] Take Chan meditation as an example.

The process by which it cuts off afflictions to the uttermost is this: ten thousand thoughts return to one (only a single thought remains in the mind, such as a huatou), one returns to nothing (not a single thought arises), one clarifies the mind and sees the nature (one thoroughly sees the original nature), and then one applies the effort of preservation until the delusions of view and thought are utterly cut off. Only thus can one end birth and death and escape rebirth. Yet its very first and easiest stage, “ten thousand thoughts return to one,” already corresponds to the single-mindedness of the Pure Land Dharma-gate. And for one who cultivates the Pure Land Dharma-gate, so long as one reaches single-mindedness, one will without fail be reborn in the highest grade in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and thereby end birth and death and escape rebirth. So it is that by Chan one may end birth and death, yet among a hundred million hardly one succeeds, whereas by Buddha-recitation ten thousand cultivate and ten thousand go. From this we know how vast and profound Amitābha Buddha’s grace and virtue are, and how rare and precious the Pure Land Dharma-gate is. Hence the Buddha said:
“The question you

ask today, Ānanda, is greater by a hundred thousand million times in merit than making offerings to the arhats and pratyekabuddhas of one world-system, or giving alms for many kalpas to the celestial beings and human beings and to the flying and wriggling creatures. Why is this? Because the celestial beings and human beings of the future and all living beings
will all, because of your question, attain deliverance because of the question you have asked
[One who is single-minded and undefiled is reborn in the highest grade]
Bodhisattva Jueming Miaoxing says:

“One who recites in this way — afflictions and worldly toils neither cut off nor bound — is simply of one mind. Only when one has surely attained single-mindedness may one truly be said to hold the Name, may one truly be said to be single-minded and undefiled; the work of the pure karma is accomplished, and one goes straight to the highest grade.”
(For details, see
Notes on A Sure Guide to the West

[Ten thousand cultivate and ten thousand go] The word “cultivate” here means true, practical cultivation with correct method and diligent effort. Those who practice blindly and wildly, or who fear difficulty and grow slack, are not included.

[In the worlds of the ten directions, the śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and all classes of beings who are born in that Buddha-land, attain the path of nirvāṇa, and are to become Buddhas, are beyond all counting. Yet in that Buddha-land all remains ever as one single dharma, without increase. Why is this? It is like the great ocean, king among waters: all waters flow onward and enter the sea, yet does the water of the great ocean increase or diminish?]

In the worlds of the ten directions, the śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and all classes of beings who are reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, attain the path to Buddhahood, and are to become Buddhas, are beyond all counting. Yet the Land of Ultimate Bliss remains ever just as it is, with no increase in the number of its people. Why is this? It is like the great ocean, king among waters: all waters flow onward and enter the sea — can the water of the great ocean be seen to increase?

[Ever as one single dharma, without increase] Though the beings of all the worlds of the ten directions who are reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss are beyond all counting, the Land of Ultimate Bliss remains ever just as it is, like the ten thousand rivers flowing into the great ocean, by which the water of the great ocean is not seen to increase. This describes the Land of Ultimate Bliss as incomparably vast and the number of its people as exceedingly, exceedingly great. In “Immeasurable Lifespan and Multitude, Chapter Thirteen,” the Buddha says:

“Among my disciples, Mahāmaudgalyāyana is foremost in spiritual power: in a single day and night he knows the number of all the stars and all the beings in the three thousand great thousand worlds. Suppose all the beings of the ten directions became pratyekabuddhas, and each pratyekabuddha had a lifespan of a trillion years and spiritual powers equal to Mahāmaudgalyāyana: exhausting their lifespans and spending all their wisdom, they might together reckon the number of śrāvakas in that Buddha's assembly, and in ten million parts they would not reach one part.”

[Whether it increase or diminish] Increase refers to those who come from the worlds of the ten directions to be reborn there; decrease refers to the bodhisattvas of the Land of Ultimate Bliss who become Buddhas and those who go to other worlds to deliver beings. However many come or go, the holy multitude of the Land of Ultimate Bliss shows neither increase nor decrease.

[Above and below and the eight directions, Buddha-lands are without number. The Land of Ultimate Bliss, long-enduring and vast, bright and fair and happy, is the most surpassing of all. This is brought about by the vows he made seeking the Way when he was a bodhisattva, and by the merit he accumulated. Amitābha Buddha's grace and virtue, bestowed throughout the eight directions, above and below, are inexhaustible and without limit, deep and vast and measureless, beyond all telling.]

Above and below and the eight directions (the ten directions), Buddha-lands are without number. Amitābha Buddha's Land of Ultimate Bliss, long-enduring and vast, bright and beautiful and fair, happy and blissful, is the most surpassing of all. All this is brought about by the vows he made seeking the Way when he was a bodhisattva, and by the merit he accumulated. Amitābha Buddha's grace and virtue, bestowed throughout the eight directions, above and below (the ten directions), are inexhaustible and without limit, deep and vast and measureless, beyond all telling.

[Again, Ānanda, all the bodhisattvas in that Buddha-land are complete in meditation and wisdom, in spiritual powers, awesome virtue, and merit; there is nothing in which they are not perfect. The secret treasury of all Buddhas they understand completely and clearly. They tame and subdue all their faculties, and their bodies and minds are gentle and harmonious. They enter deeply into right wisdom and have no remaining habits. Following what the Buddha practiced, they cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment and the noble path.]

Again, Ānanda: all the bodhisattvas in the Land of Ultimate Bliss are complete in meditation and wisdom, in spiritual powers, awesome virtue, and merit; there is nothing in which they are not perfect. The secret treasury of all Buddhas (that is, the original nature) they understand completely and clearly. They tame and subdue all their faculties, and their bodies (their conduct) and minds are gentle and harmonious. They enter deeply into right wisdom and no longer have any habits. Following what the Buddha taught, they cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment and the noble eightfold path.

[Gentle and harmonious] Body (conduct) and mind are soft and compliant with the Way, not hard and stubborn, difficult to transform. [Remaining habits] The residual habitual tendencies left after afflictions are cut off, or simply called habits. [The seven factors of enlightenment] That is, the seven branches of enlightenment, also called the seven factors of bodhi, the seven limbs of enlightenment, and the seven equal-enlightenment limbs: the seven kinds of awakening brought forth by the five roots and the five powers. 1. The enlightenment factor of discerning the Dharma, that is, using wisdom to discern the true from the false in dharmas; 2. the enlightenment factor of vigor, that is, with a courageous mind vigorously practicing the right Dharma; 3. the enlightenment factor of joy, that is, the mind attaining the good Dharma and giving rise to joy; 4. the enlightenment factor of ease, that is, removing the coarse and heavy afflictions of body and mind and attaining lightness and comfort; 5. the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, that is, constantly mindful and contemplating the right Dharma, so that concentration and wisdom are equal; 6. the enlightenment factor of concentration, that is, the mind abiding on a single object without distraction; 7. the enlightenment factor of equanimity, that is, renouncing all false dharmas and vigorously practicing the right Dharma. [The five roots] The root of faith, the root of effort, the root of mindfulness, the root of concentration, and the root of wisdom. Because these five dharmas are the root from which the noble path is born, they are called the “five roots.” [The five powers] When the five roots are firm and generate strength, they are called the “five powers”: the power of faith, the power of effort, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. The power of faith is the growth of the root of faith, able to destroy all wrong faiths; the power of effort is the growth of the root of effort, able to destroy the laziness of body and mind; the power of mindfulness is the growth of the root of mindfulness, able to destroy all wrong thoughts; the power of concentration is the growth of the root of concentration, able to destroy all confused thinking; the power of wisdom is the growth of the root of wisdom, able to destroy all the delusions of the three realms.

[The noble eightfold path] Also called the eight right paths: the eight ways of the noble ones. 1. Right view, correct understanding. 2. Right thought, correct thinking. 3. Right speech, proper speech. 4. Right action, proper conduct. 5. Right livelihood, a proper profession or way of life. 6. Right effort, proper endeavor. 7. Right mindfulness, correct recollection. 8. Right concentration, correct meditative absorption.

[Cultivating the five eyes, they illumine the true and penetrate the conventional. The flesh eye discerns, the heaven eye penetrates, the Dharma eye is pure, the wisdom eye sees the true, the Buddha eye is complete, awakening to the nature of all dharmas.]

They cultivate the five eyes, illumining the true and penetrating the conventional. The flesh eye discerns (it is able to distinguish well the characteristics of all dharmas); the heaven eye penetrates (near and far, obstructed and unobstructed, day and night are no hindrance); the Dharma eye is pure (it comprehends all Dharma-gates of the world and beyond the world); the wisdom eye sees the true (it sees through false appearances and knows true emptiness); the Buddha eye is complete (there is nothing it does not know, nothing it does not see), awakening to the true character of all dharmas.
The Sutra of Immeasurable Life as Spoken by the Buddha (the Wei translation) says:

“The flesh eye is pure and clear, nothing is not distinguished; the heaven eye penetrates, immeasurable and boundless; the Dharma eye observes, penetrating all paths to the end; the wisdom eye sees the true and can cross to the other shore; the Buddha eye is complete, awakening to the nature of all dharmas.”

[The five eyes] The flesh eye, the heaven eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye. The flesh eye is the eye of ordinary beings with physical bodies: meeting darkness or meeting obstruction, it cannot see. The heaven eye is the eye of celestial beings: near and far, obstructed and unobstructed, day and night, it can see them all. The wisdom eye is the eye of the śrāvakas: it can see through false appearances and know true emptiness. The Dharma eye is the eye of the bodhisattvas: it can comprehend all Dharma-gates of the world and beyond the world. The Buddha eye is the eye of the Tathāgata: having the Buddha eye, one also possesses the four preceding eyes, and can know all things and see all things; amid all dharmas, the Buddha eye constantly illumines.

[Illumine the true and penetrate the conventional] To illumine the true character of all dharmas and to penetrate the myriad phenomena. By illumining the true, one's own practice is perfected and reaches the ultimate; by penetrating the conventional, one sets forth teachings according to capacity and delivers measureless beings. The Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sutra says:
“He is able to distinguish well the characteristics of all dharmas, yet in the supreme meaning he does not move.”
[The supreme meaning] That is, the supreme meaning truth, the highest, unsurpassed, perfect, and ultimate truth. The true character of all dharmas is the supreme meaning truth. The Buddha says:

“All dharmas are false; where they cease, that is called the real, that is called the true character, that is called the Dharma realm, called ultimate wisdom, called the supreme meaning truth, called the supreme meaning emptiness.”
(The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra)

[Retaining all eloquence, free and unobstructed. Skillfully understanding the world, with boundless skillful means. What they say is true and real, entering deeply into the flavor of the meaning. Delivering all sentient beings, they expound the right Dharma. Without marks, without contrivance, without bondage, without liberation. Without any discriminations, far removed from inversion. In all that they enjoy, they grasp at nothing.]

These bodhisattvas are complete in all eloquence, free and unobstructed. They skillfully understand the boundless skillful means of the world. What they say is sincere and true (true and real), entering deeply into the flavor of the meaning. They deliver all beings and expound the right Dharma. Without marks, without contrivance, without bondage, without liberation. Without any discriminations, far removed from inversion. In all that they enjoy, they grasp at nothing.
[Retaining all eloquence] Retaining every kind of eloquence, that is, being complete in all eloquence. The Sutra of Immeasurable Life as Spoken by the Buddha (the Wei translation) says:
“They are complete in all eloquence.”

[Skillful means] The devices, methods, or words adopted in order to guide and teach beings. What is called “skillful means” is spoken in contrast to the real (the true character of all dharmas). [Without marks, without contrivance] That is, as the Diamond Sutra says:

“All the various kinds of living beings — whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether with form or without form; whether with thought, without thought, or neither with thought nor without thought — I cause them all to enter nirvāṇa without remainder and be delivered
— that is, I shall deliver them all to Buddhahood —
and thus I deliver measureless, countless, boundless beings
— thus delivering measureless, countless, boundless beings to Buddhahood —
yet in truth no being whatsoever is delivered
— yet in truth there is no such thing as a being who is delivered and becomes a Buddha
(For the notes, see, in detail,
The Diamond Sutra, Explained
[Without marks] That is, not clinging to marks. The Diamond Sutra says:
“Whatever has marks is false and delusive.”
(For the notes, see, in detail,
The Diamond Sutra, Explained

) [Clinging to marks] Taking marks as real, so that one has love and hate, acceptance and rejection, and is entangled by them. [Without bondage, without liberation] There is neither bondage nor liberation. The world takes ignorance and affliction as bondage, and the cutting off of delusion and the revealing of the true as liberation. But these bodhisattvas have awakened to the nature of dharmas and clearly understand that the essence of the false and the true is one; they enter the Dharma-gate of non-duality, and therefore there is for them neither bondage nor liberation.

[The Dharma-gate of non-duality] The Dharma-gate of non-duality. This is the ultimate teaching that transcends relativity and difference. Above the eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates of Buddhism, it is that by which one may directly see the noble path.

[Roaming everywhere through the Buddha-lands, without love and without aversion. They have no thought of seeking or not seeking, and no thought of self and other, of opposition and resentment. Why is this? Because those bodhisattvas have a mind of great compassion that benefits all beings. They renounce all clinging and accomplish measureless merit.]

With an equal mind they roam everywhere through the Buddha-lands, universally delivering beings, without love and without aversion. They have no thought of seeking or not seeking, and no thought of self and other, of opposition and anger and resentment. Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas have a mind of great compassion that benefits all beings. They renounce all clinging and accomplish measureless merit.

[With unobstructed wisdom, they understand dharmas as thus. They well know the origin and the cessation, and the skillful means of voice. They take no delight in worldly talk, but rejoice in right discourse. They know all dharmas to be utterly empty and still. The afflictions of the body born of birth, the two remainders, are wholly exhausted. In the three realms they cultivate diligently with an equal mind, penetrating the One Vehicle to the end and reaching the other shore.]

With unobstructed wisdom (wisdom perfect and penetrating), they understand all dharmas as thus, and skillfully expound the right Dharma (well knowing the origin and the cessation, and the skillful means of voice). They take no delight in the world's useless talk, but take their joy solely in the ultimate and definitive teachings of the Mahāyāna (rejoicing in right discourse). They know all dharmas to be utterly empty and still. The fruits of suffering of the body born of birth and the residual habits of affliction are wholly gone. In the three realms they cultivate diligently with an equal mind, penetrating the One Vehicle Dharma (the sole teaching that can bring a person to Buddhahood) to the end, until they attain Buddhahood.

[Thus] Thusness as the true suchness. This is the self-nature's own realm, which is unmoving, still and silent, equal and non-dual, and free of inverted discrimination. [True suchness] “True” means real and not false; “thus” means unchanging. Combining the two meanings of real-and-not-false and unchanging, it is called “true suchness,” and true suchness is the true character of all dharmas. [Well knowing the origin and the cessation, and the skillful means of voice] “Origin and cessation” refers to the Four Noble Truths of the origin of suffering and the cessation of suffering, and “the skillful means of voice” means being able to expound skillfully. [Truth] A principle that is real and without error.

[The Four Noble Truths] The truth of suffering, the truth of the origin of suffering, the truth of the cessation of suffering, and the truth of the path. 1. The “truth of suffering” is the truth that explains the many sufferings of human life. Suffering has oppression as its mark. Human life has three sufferings, eight sufferings, and measureless sufferings; suffering is the reality of actual human life. 2. In the “truth of origin,” “origin” means to bring about or to cause; it is the truth that explains how the sufferings of human life come to be. The pain of human life is due to craving, and so one grasps, and so one creates karma, and so one suffers, and so one is reborn. 3. The “truth of cessation” is the truth that explains the stilling of all sufferings. When all the origin of suffering (craving) is cut off forever without remainder, with no grasping and no clinging, then one no longer creates karma, suffers, or is reborn — this is the truth of cessation. 4. The “truth of the path” is the truth that explains how to cut off the origin of suffering (craving) forever, that is, the path of the cessation of suffering. Among the Four Noble Truths, origin is the cause and suffering is the fruit; the path is the cause and cessation is the fruit.
[Born of birth]

The bodies of all Buddhas and bodhisattvas are of two kinds: the Dharma-body and the body born of birth. The essential principle they realize is called the “Dharma-body,” while the fleshly body, born from a mother's womb in order to rescue and deliver beings, is called the “body born of birth.” [The two remainders] The fruits of suffering of the body born of birth and the residual habits of affliction are called the two remainders.

[Cutting through the net of doubt, they realize that there is nothing to be obtained. With the wisdom of skillful means they increase their understanding. From the very beginning they abide in the spiritual penetrations, attain the One Vehicle path, and are not awakened by any other means.]

They cut through the net of doubt and realize the state in which, in truth, there is no dharma whatsoever to be obtained. With the wisdom of skillful means they increase their understanding. From the very root they abide in the spiritual penetrations, attain the One Vehicle path, and awaken to the Way and become Buddhas.
[Realizing that there is nothing to be obtained] This is the cutting off of the attachment to dharmas.
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
“This ignorance has no real substance of its own, like a person in a dream: while dreaming, it is not nothing, but when he awakes, there is nothing at all to be obtained.”
(For the notes, see, in detail,
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, Explained

[Attachment to dharmas] Clinging to all dharmas as truly existing; it is one of the two attachments (the attachment to self and the attachment to dharmas). [Attachment to self] Clinging to body and mind as “I.” [The wisdom of skillful means] Also called the wisdom of expedients, in contrast to the wisdom of the real. To penetrate the true character of all dharmas is called the wisdom of the real; to understand thoroughly the differences among the myriad phenomena is called the wisdom of expedients (the wisdom of skillful means). [Not awakened by any other means] To awaken to the Way and become a Buddha not by any other path (but by the One Vehicle path).

[Their wisdom is vast and profound, like the great sea. Their bodhi is lofty and broad, likened to Mount Sumeru. Their own awesome radiance surpasses the sun and moon. Their minds are pure white, like snowy mountains. Their patience is like the earth, equal toward all. Their purity is like water, washing away all dust and defilement. Their blazing intensity is like fire, burning the firewood of affliction. Their non-clinging is like the wind, without any obstruction.]

The bodhisattvas of the Land of Ultimate Bliss have wisdom vast and profound, like the great sea. Their bodhi mind is lofty and broad, like Mount Sumeru. Their own awesome radiance surpasses the sun and moon. Their minds are pure white, like snowy mountains. Their patience is like the great earth, equal toward all. Body (conduct) and mind are pure like water, washing away all dust and defilement. Their wisdom blazes like fire, cutting off affliction as fire burns firewood. Their non-clinging (not clinging to marks) is like the wind, without any obstruction.

[Patience like the earth] This uses the great earth as a simile for the patience that is equal (free of all discrimination). The great earth bears all things — heavy and light, pure and foul — with one and the same load, making no choice and no distinction. This is used to illustrate the bodhisattva's virtue of patience, which is free of all distinctions of self and other, of favor and grudge, of opposition and compliance. [Dust and defilement] A general term for affliction. [Blazing like fire, burning the firewood of affliction] Fire illustrates wisdom, and firewood illustrates affliction.

[The thunder of the Dharma-voice awakens those not yet awakened. They rain down the sweet-dew Dharma to nourish beings. They are vast as space, because their great compassion is equal. They are like a pure lotus, because they are free of defilement. They are like the nyagrodha tree, because their shade shelters many. They are like the vajra club, because they shatter wrong clinging. They are like the Iron Ring Mountain, because all demons and heterodox teachers cannot move them.]

When they expound the sutras and teach the Dharma, the thunder of the Dharma-voice awakens those not yet awakened. They rain down the sweet-dew Dharma to nourish beings. They are broad and boundless as space, because their great compassion is equal. They are like a pure lotus, because they are free of defilement. They are like the nyagrodha tree, because they shelter and protect a great many beings. They are like the vajra club, because they shatter wrong clinging. They are like the Iron Ring Mountain, because all demons and heterodox teachers cannot shake them.
[The sweet-dew Dharma] The Treatise on the Buddha-ground says:

“The Tathāgata's holy teaching, among all the heterodox paths and all the world's inferior and crooked teachings, is the most real. Surpassingly pure, like ghee and like sweet dew, it brings one to nirvāṇa.”
[The nyagrodha tree] The Sutra of the Retribution of Sin and Merit says:
“The nyagrodha
tuó
tree is twenty li tall, its branches spread out round, and it shades sixty li. The fruit on that tree numbers tens of thousands of hu.”

[Their minds are upright and straightforward, skillful and decisive. They discourse on the Dharma without weariness and seek the Dharma without fatigue. Their precepts are like crystal, bright and pure within and without. What they say delights and convinces the assembly. They beat the Dharma drum, raise the Dharma banner, shine the sun of wisdom, and shatter the darkness of delusion. Pure and gentle, still and discerning. They are great guiding teachers, taming and subduing self and others. They guide the multitude of beings to renounce all love and clinging and forever leave the three defilements, sporting in the spiritual penetrations.]

Their minds are upright and without selfishness, skillful and firm. They discourse on the Dharma without weariness and seek the Dharma without fatigue. Their observance of the precepts is like crystal, bright and pure within and without. What they say makes the great assembly delight and submit. They beat the Dharma drum, raise the Dharma banner, and shine the sun of wisdom to shatter the beings' darkness of delusion and ignorance. Pure (meaning that the bodhisattvas' minds are clear and free of defilement) and gentle, still and discerning. They are great guiding teachers, taming and subduing self and others. Skillfully and without obstruction they guide beings to renounce all craving and clinging and forever leave the three defilements (greed, anger, and delusion).

[The Dharma banner] A simile for the wondrous Dharma held high, like a banner hung aloft. [The sun of wisdom] The wisdom that illumines all things. [The three defilements] Another name for the three poisons, namely greed, anger, and delusion. [Sporting in the spiritual penetrations] This means that Buddhas and bodhisattvas freely and at play gather and transform beings by means of spiritual penetrations, taking that as their delight. Here “sporting in the spiritual penetrations” depicts the skillful and unobstructed way in which the bodhisattvas of the Land of Ultimate Bliss “guide the multitude of beings to renounce all love and clinging and forever leave the three defilements.”

[By the powers of cause, condition, and vow, they bring forth roots of virtue, crush and subdue all armies of demons, and revere and serve all Buddhas. They are a bright lamp for the world and the supreme field of merit. Surpassingly auspicious, they are worthy to receive offerings. Radiant and joyful, heroic and fearless. Their bodily forms and marks are fair, their merit and eloquence complete and adorned, and there is none to equal them. They are constantly praised in common by all Buddhas. They perfect all the bodhisattva pāramitās, and constantly abide in the samādhis of neither birth nor extinction. Their practice pervades the place of enlightenment, and they are far from the realm of the Two Vehicles.]

These bodhisattvas, by the power of cause, the power of condition, and the power of vow, bring forth roots of virtue, crush and subdue all armies of demons, and revere and serve all Buddhas. They are a bright lamp that shatters the world's darkness and the supreme field of merit for beings. Surpassingly auspicious, they are worthy to receive offerings. Their bearing is radiant and joyful, their body and mind heroic and fearless. Their bodily forms and marks are fair, their merit and eloquence complete and adorned, and there is none to equal them. They are constantly praised in common by all Buddhas. They penetrate all the bodhisattva pāramitās, and constantly abide in the samādhis of neither birth nor extinction. In the practice of the place of enlightenment nothing is lacking (their practice pervades the place of enlightenment), and they are far from the realm of the Two Vehicles (the śrāvaka vehicle and the pratyekabuddha vehicle), relying solely on the One Vehicle Dharma.

[The power of cause] The fundamental power by which all things are produced. It is the counterpart of the “power of condition.” The Sutra of the Assembly of Immeasurable Life (the Tang translation) says:
“The power of cause, the power of condition, the power of vow.”
[The power of condition] The power of assisting conditions. It is spoken in contrast to the power of cause. Huiyuan's Commentary says:
“To draw near good teachers and hear the right Dharma is called the power of condition.
” [The power of vow] The power of solemn vows.

[The field of merit] Making offerings and giving alms, doing good and cultivating virtue, one can receive the reward of blessing, just as sowing a field brings the profit of the autumn harvest: in spring one grain of millet is sown, in autumn ten thousand seeds are reaped. [Radiant] The appearance of shining glory.

[Ānanda, I now speak in brief: the true merit and virtue of the bodhisattvas born in that Land of Ultimate Bliss are all like this. Were one to speak of them at length, a hundred thousand million kalpas could not exhaust them.]

Ānanda, I now speak in brief of the true merit and virtue of the bodhisattvas who are reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss: all of it is like this. Were one to speak of it at length, then a hundred thousand million kalpas could not exhaust it.

[The Buddha told Bodhisattva Maitreya and the celestial beings and others: In the land of Immeasurable Life, the merit and wisdom of the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas cannot be described, and its land is subtle, blissful, and pure as this. Why do you not strive to do good and be mindful of the Way, the natural?]

The Buddha told Bodhisattva Maitreya and the celestial beings and others: In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the merit and wisdom of the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas cannot be described (this is the direct reward), and moreover the land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss is subtle, blissful, and pure as this (this is the dependent reward). Why then do you not strive with all your might to do good, single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name, and seek rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss?

This passage urges and entreats one to seek rebirth: the direct reward and the dependent reward of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss are so incomparably surpassing — why not strive with all one’s might to do good and seek rebirth there?

[Subtle, blissful, and pure] Adorned beyond all compare, hence “subtle”; free of all affliction, hence “blissful”; free of all entanglement, hence “pure.” [Doing good] “Doing good” here refers to the good conduct of one who recites the Buddha’s name: holding the Name in recitation is the root of goodness and the primary practice of “doing good”; cutting off evil and cultivating good is the auxiliary practice of “doing good.” [Mindful of the Way, the natural] The Land of Ultimate Bliss is an unconditioned, natural world; those reborn in that land at once receive a natural, ethereal body. Therefore “the natural” here refers to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. “Of” means “going toward.” “Mindful of the Way” means the mind abiding on the Way; for one who recites the Buddha’s name, it means the mind abiding on the Buddha’s Name. “Mindful of the Way, the natural” means the mind abiding on the Buddha’s Name and seeking rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. But here “doing good” means the good conduct of one who recites the Buddha’s name. Master Shandao says:
“If one can keep the recitation continuous, thought after thought, with the end of life as the limit, then ten recite and ten are reborn, a hundred recite and a hundred are reborn.”
(For details, see
Master Shandao’s Pure Land Teaching

[Going out and coming in to make offerings, contemplating the sutras and walking the Way, they delight in them and practice them long. Their talents are keen and their wisdom sharp, their minds do not turn back, and their intent knows no slackening. Outwardly they seem slow and leisurely, inwardly they alone race on. Vast and capacious as space, they perfectly attain the middle. Inner and outer correspond, and naturally they are solemn and orderly. Restrained and upright, body and mind are pure.]

The holy multitude of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, in going out and coming in to make offerings (cultivating merit), and in contemplating the sutras and walking the Way (cultivating wisdom), all delight in them and practice them long. Their talents are keen and their wisdom bright, their minds do not retreat (their minds do not turn back), and their intent knows no time of slackening. Outwardly they are broad, relaxed, and at ease, as though they had nothing to do, yet inwardly they advance without cease, pure thoughts continuing one after another. Though they advance without cease, their minds are like space, holding not a single thing, which is exactly the middle way. Inner (the mind) and outer (the conduct) correspond, and naturally they are solemn and orderly; restrained (collected) and upright, body and mind are pure.

[Going out and coming in to make offerings] Flying and transforming to the places of the Buddhas of the ten directions (going out), making offerings to all the Buddhas, and then returning to the Land of Ultimate Bliss (coming in).

[The middle way] Not leaning toward emptiness (advancing without cease) nor toward existence (holding not a single thing); neither empty nor existent, both empty and existent, falling into neither extreme, perfect and unobstructed.

[They have no love or greed, their vows and aspirations are settled. They neither increase nor diminish, but seek the Way in harmony and rectitude. They are not misled into the crooked, but follow the sutras and keep the commandments. They dare not stumble, as if before the inked line. All aspire to the Way, vast and free of other thoughts. They have no sorrow or anxiety, and are naturally unconditioned. Like space, they stand nowhere, calm and at peace without desire.]

They have no love or greed, and their vows are firm. They are not sometimes hot and sometimes cold (neither increasing nor diminishing), but seek the Way in harmony and uprightness. They are not misled by biased views and false teachings, but strictly follow the words of the sutras and the precepts (following the sutras and keeping the commandments). They dare not make the slightest error, like a carpenter following the inked line. With all their strength they aspire to the supreme Way, and their minds are vast and free of delusive thoughts. They have no sorrow or anxiety, and are naturally unconditioned. Their minds are like space, in which not a single dharma is established; they are tranquil and at peace, with nothing to desire.
[Love and greed] To be steeped and stained is “love.” The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
“Know that love is the root of rebirth.”
To desire and seek is “greed.”
The Lotus Sutra says:
“Greed and desire are the root of all suffering; if greed and desire are extinguished, there is no support for suffering
(the cause of suffering has nothing to rest upon)
[The inked line] A carpenter inks a cord with black and snaps a straight line on the wood as the guide for sawing and planing. It is a simile for rules and standards.

The next two passages describe the realm of the beings of the Land of Ultimate Bliss who have clarified the mind and seen the nature. Clarifying the mind and seeing the nature (thoroughly seeing the original nature) is what the Chan school strives after with all its might; it is extremely difficult and few succeed. But for one reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, it becomes a matter of course, without a single exception. Therefore Master Yongming’s Four Selections says:
“Once one sees Amitābha, why worry that one will not awaken
(clarify the mind and see the nature)

[Accomplishing good vows, they seek with all their hearts. Harboring compassion and pity, they accord with propriety and righteousness, embracing within and without, and cross over to deliverance. Naturally they preserve and guard; truly, truly pure and white, their vows are supreme, and they are serene, settled, and at peace.]

They accomplish good vows and seek with all their hearts. With great compassion and pity (harboring compassion and pity), they fully accord with the world’s propriety, law, and righteousness, and are perfect in both principle and phenomena (embracing within and without), attaining deliverance. Guarding the mind-nature, not a single thought arises (truly, truly pure and white), their vows are supreme, and they are serene, settled, and at peace.

[Good vows] That is, what was said earlier in “Paying Homage and Making Offerings, Hearing the Dharma, Chapter Twenty-Six”: “They aspire to adorn the pure lands (taking Amitābha Buddha as their model and resolving to take in a Buddha-land as adorned and pure as the Land of Ultimate Bliss).”
[Accomplishing good vows, they seek with all their hearts] “Sincere Diligence, Chapter Five” says:
“They formed great vows and sought with diligent devotion.”

[Embracing within and without] “Without” refers to the phenomenal aspect, and “within” to the essential principle. To embrace both within and without is to perfect both principle and phenomena. [Crossing over] Means to be delivered. The Sutra of Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment as Spoken by the Buddha (the Han translation) says:

“The celestial beings and human beings in all the worlds of the eight directions, above and below, who are crossed over, and the flying and wriggling creatures, are all caused to attain the Buddha’s path of nirvāṇa.”

[Once they open through and clearly penetrate, there is the natural within the natural, the root and source of the natural, and the natural’s light and color interweaving and turning, transforming into the most surpassing. Yudan becomes the seven treasures, and all things are gathered and formed; pure radiance and essence all emerge together, good and fair beyond all compare. They settle in neither above nor below, and penetrate without bound.]

Once they suddenly awaken (clarify the mind and see the nature), they see the natural within the natural, the root and source of the natural (the myriad phenomena) — that is, the true character of all dharmas — and the natural’s light and color, turning and revolving like the stars, transform into the most surpassing. All things flow forth naturally from the one great treasury of radiance,
wondrous radiance shining forth brilliantly,
surpassing beyond all compare. No longer clinging to distinctions of above and below, pure and impure, and the like, they penetrate all things without bound.
[Opening through and clearly penetrating] To clarify the mind and see the nature, that is, to see the original nature thoroughly. Concerning self-nature and original nature, see, in detail,
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathāgatagarbha
— that article. [Turning and revolving] shen (

) hui and dou zhuan: shen is the Shen star, dou is the Northern Dipper. [The natural’s light and color interweaving and turning, transforming into the most surpassing] This describes the realm of entering a new heaven and a new earth through clarifying the mind and seeing the nature.
[Yudan becomes the seven treasures, and all things are gathered and formed; pure radiance and essence all emerge together, good and fair beyond all compare] This is to say:
all things flow forth naturally from the one great treasury of radiance,
wondrous radiance shining forth brilliantly,
surpassing beyond all compare.
Master Hanshan says:
“When you see the place where not a single thought arises
(truly, truly pure and white)
, then the preceding and succeeding limits are cut off, and the middle stands alone. Suddenly the lacquer bucket is smashed, and you at once see your original face
(thoroughly seeing the original nature)
. Then body, mind, and world all at once sink away, like the shadow of a sky-flower falling
(the illusory shadow of the sky-flower ceases)
, and the ten directions are perfectly bright, forming one great treasury of radiance.”
(The Dream-Roaming Collection,
“The Essentials of Buddha-Recitation and Chan Contemplation”)
[The preceding and succeeding limits] The preceding limit refers to the past, the succeeding limit to the future. The Jingying Commentary says:
“Conditioned dharmas arise one after another. The former is the preceding limit, the latter the succeeding limit.”

[When the preceding and succeeding limits are cut off, the middle stands alone] With no former thought and no latter thought, the state of lucid, solitary awareness is the realm in which not a single thought arises. The Record of the Mirror of the Source says:

“If not a single thought arises, then the preceding and succeeding limits are cut off. The illuminating essence stands alone, things and self are both thus, and one goes straight to the source of the mind.”
The Prefaces to the Collected Writings on the Sources of Chan says:
“Hearing once, one awakens to a thousand; one gains the great retention; not a single thought arises, and the preceding and succeeding limits are cut off.”
[Sinking away]
Also written “sinking away”: to vanish, to disappear.
The Sutra of Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment Spoken by the Buddha (Han translation) says:

“Once one opens through and attains clear comprehension, within the natural there is the mark of the natural, and the natural has its root and foundation. Naturally there come to be five lights up to nine colors; the five lights up to nine colors intermingle and revolve, changing through hundreds and thousands of transformations — the most surpassing naturalness. Naturally the seven treasures are formed, gathered and clasped into all things; the lights and essences intermingle in brightness, all bringing forth excellence, of a beauty beyond all measure.”
The Sutra of Amitābha, the Perfectly Awakened Buddha of the Sala Grove, Who Delivers Beings on the Human Path (Wu translation) says:
“In the naturalness of Uttarakuru, the seven treasures are naturally formed, gathered and clasped into all things.”
“Uttarakuru”:

Uttarakuru, also written Auttarakuru, is the northern continent of Uttarakuru. “The northern continent of Uttarakuru”: it is one of the four great continents of the Sahā world (Pūrvavideha in the east, Jambudvīpa in the south, Aparagodānīya in the west, and Uttarakuru in the north), lying to the north of Mount Sumeru, where the people are peaceful and happy and live a thousand years. “Uttarakuru becomes the seven treasures, gathered and clasped into all things”: the prelude to seeing one’s nature clearly (to penetratingly beholding the intrinsic nature) is the non-arising of a single thought (what the text above calls “truly pure and undefiled”); the state at that time is peaceful and happy (what the text above calls “calm samādhi and peace”), and so Uttarakuru, the northern continent whose people are peaceful and happy, is used as a simile. Once one sees one’s nature clearly (“once one opens through and attains clear comprehension”) and enters the realm of a new heaven and a new earth, this is a leap in kind; hence the transformation “Uttarakuru becomes the seven treasures” is used as a simile. “Gathered and clasped into all things” describes how at that time all things flow forth naturally from the one great treasury of radiance.
The passage below once again urges and exhorts us toward rebirth. This is the World-Honored One’s repeated admonition, his compassion without end.

“Each should strive with diligence, and seek the Way by his own effort. You shall surely transcend and pass beyond, reborn in the land of Amitābha, immeasurable and pure. Cutting across the five destinies, the evil paths close of themselves. The unsurpassed and wondrous Way is easy to go, yet none go there; that land turns no one away — it is the natural pull that draws them on. Let go your aims as though they were empty space, and diligently walk the Way, seeking its virtue. You may gain life beyond measure, with bliss and years that have no end. Why cling to the affairs of the world, why such
náo
clamor — the worry over impermanence?”

The Land of Ultimate Bliss is so surpassing that each of you should strive with diligence, and seek rebirth there by his own effort. You shall surely transcend the three realms and be reborn in the land of Amitābha, immeasurable and pure — the Land of Ultimate Bliss — and so escape the six paths of rebirth.
